# How to use this guide

Social Pharmacy is a theory-heavy, "write what you understand" subject. There are no reactions or calculations to memorise, but there are many **definitions, lists, tables and disease facts**. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, write the "Remember" list from memory, then answer the question bank without looking.

**Where the marks are.** Unit 4 (microbiology, epidemiology and communicable diseases) takes about 28 of the 75 teaching hours, so expect the most questions from it. Next come Unit 2 (preventive healthcare, about 18 hours) and Unit 3 (nutrition, about 10 hours). Units 1 and 5 give steady long and short questions; Unit 6 (pharmacoeconomics) usually gives one short question or a few objective ones.

**Exam pattern.** Under PCI Education Regulations 2020, each D.Pharm theory subject carries **100 marks: 20 sessional (internal) + 80 in the yearly board exam, 3 hours**. In Himachal Pradesh the yearly exam is conducted by HPTSB. The usual ER-2020 board paper is set out below, and the mock paper in this guide follows it. Boards can vary it, so **confirm the pattern with your college**.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| I | Objective questions — answer all | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| II | Short answers — answer 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| III | Long answers — answer 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |
| | **Total** | **80** |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a topic asked in most years or carrying big syllabus weight; prepare the full answer.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for objective questions and as a backup choice.

The rating is an estimate from common exam patterns and syllabus weight. It is not a promise.

**Scoring tips for Social Pharmacy**

1. **Start with a definition.** Health, epidemiology, quarantine, balanced diet, pharmacoeconomics — a clear one-line definition earns the first mark.
2. **Use a fixed format for every disease:** causative agent → mode of spread → incubation period → clinical features → treatment → prevention → role of pharmacist. Examiners look for each heading.
3. **Draw tables and simple diagrams:** the epidemiological triad, three-tier health system, classification of contraceptives, types of immunity, colour coding of bio-medical waste.
4. **Always end with "Role of the pharmacist"** in 4–6 points. It is the purpose of the subject, and many papers ask it directly.
5. **Quote Indian examples:** NHM, NTEP, Ni-kshay, Jan Aushadhi, COTPA 2003, NDPS Act 1985, FSSAI, IMS Act, Mission Indradhanush.
6. **Write numbers only when you are sure:** fast-breathing cut-offs, ORS osmolarity 245, residual chlorine 0.5 mg/L, cold chain +2 to +8 °C, breastfeeding within 1 hour and exclusive for 6 months.
7. **Practise the very short questions aloud** — they are quick 2-mark wins (e.g. "Define incubation period", "Name two live vaccines").

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, master these: **WHO definition and dimensions of health**, **three-tier health system and NHM**, **family planning methods**, **breastfeeding vs bottle feeding**, **types of immunity and vaccines with cold chain**, **balanced diet and deficiency diseases**, **food adulteration**, **epidemiology terms**, **TB, malaria, dengue, cholera/diarrhoea, HIV**, **NTEP and NVBDCP**, and **the four types of pharmacoeconomic analysis**.

**Unit 1 — Introduction**

| Item | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Social Pharmacy | Social, behavioural, economic factors in medicine use + pharmacist's public-health role |
| WHO health (1948) | Complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease |
| Dimensions | Physical, mental, social, spiritual, emotional, vocational |
| Determinants | Biology, lifestyle, environment, socio-economic, health services |
| IMR | Infant deaths < 1 yr per 1000 live births; best single health indicator |
| MMR | Maternal deaths per 1,00,000 live births |
| Population norms | Sub-centre 5,000 / PHC 30,000 / CHC 1,20,000 (hilly 3,000 / 20,000 / 80,000) |
| NHM | NRHM 2005 + NUHM 2013; ASHA, JSY, JSSK, RBSK, RKSK |
| NHP 2017 | Wellness, Health and Wellness Centres, free drugs and diagnostics |
| Goals | MDGs 8 (2000–15); SDGs 17 (2015–30), SDG 3 = health; FIP DGs 21 (2020) |

**Unit 2 — Preventive healthcare**

| Item | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Demographic cycle | 5 stages; India late expanding; replacement TFR 2.1 |
| Contraceptives | Barrier, IUD (Cu-T 380A ~10 yr), pills (Mala-N), centchroman (Chhaya), DMPA (Antara, 3-monthly), ECP within 72 h, vasectomy/tubectomy |
| Breastfeeding | Within 1 hour, colostrum, exclusive 6 months, continue 2 years; IMS Act 1992 |
| Immunity | Active (natural/artificial) vs passive (maternal/immunoglobulin) |
| Live vaccines | BCG, OPV, MR, rotavirus, varicella; toxoids = tetanus, diphtheria |
| Cold chain | +2 to +8 °C; VVM shows heat damage; shake test for freezing |
| Water | Residual chlorine 0.5 mg/L after 1 h; bleaching powder ~33% available chlorine |
| BMW 2016 | Yellow (incinerate), red (plastics), white (sharps), blue (glass) |
| Noise | Above ~85 dB damages hearing |
| Pharma pollution | AMR, fish feminisation, diclofenac and vultures; take-back, never flush |
| Abuse laws | NDPS Act 1985; COTPA 2003; Tele-MANAS 14416 |

**Unit 3 — Nutrition**

| Item | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Energy | Carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal/g |
| Kwashiorkor vs marasmus | Oedema, "red boy", fatty liver vs wasting, "old man" face, no oedema |
| Vitamins | A night blindness; D rickets; B1 beriberi; B3 pellagra (3 Ds); C scurvy; folate/B12 megaloblastic anaemia |
| Minerals | Iron anaemia; iodine goitre; fluoride excess fluorosis |
| Adulteration | Argemone oil → epidemic dropsy; khesari dal → lathyrism; metanil yellow in turmeric |
| Ripening | Calcium carbide (acetylene, arsenic) banned; ethylene allowed |
| Fortification | Iodised and double-fortified salt, fortified rice, oil and milk with A and D; "+F" logo |
| Drug–food | Tetracycline + milk; MAOI + cheese; warfarin + green leaves; metronidazole + alcohol; grapefruit + felodipine |

**Unit 4 — Diseases at a glance**

| Disease | Agent | Spread | Key feature | Key prevention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Chickenpox | Varicella-zoster virus | Droplet, contact | Itchy crops of vesicles | Varicella vaccine |
| Measles | Measles virus | Airborne | Koplik's spots, 3 Cs | MR vaccine, vitamin A |
| Diphtheria | C. diphtheriae | Droplet | Grey membrane, bull neck | Pentavalent/DPT |
| Pertussis | B. pertussis | Droplet | Whoop | Pentavalent/DPT |
| TB | M. tuberculosis | Droplet nuclei | Cough ≥ 2 weeks | BCG, case finding, 2HRZE/4HRE |
| Polio | Poliovirus | Faeco-oral | Acute flaccid paralysis | OPV, IPV |
| Cholera | V. cholerae | Water | Rice-water stools | Safe water, ORS |
| Typhoid | S. Typhi | Food, water | Step-ladder fever | Safe water, vaccine |
| Dengue | DENV 1–4 | Aedes (day) | Break-bone fever, low platelets | No NSAIDs, remove breeding sites |
| Malaria | Plasmodium | Anopheles (night) | Fever with chills | Nets, ACT / chloroquine + primaquine |
| Filariasis | W. bancrofti | Culex | Elephantiasis | MDA (DEC + albendazole) |
| Tetanus | C. tetani | Soil into wounds | Lockjaw | Td, clean delivery |
| Leprosy | M. leprae | Prolonged contact | Anaesthetic patch | MDT |
| HIV | Retrovirus | Sex, blood, mother–child | CD4 loss, AIDS | Condoms, ART, PPTCT |

Isolation = sick people; quarantine = healthy contacts. Triad = agent, host, environment. Diarrhoea = low-osmolarity ORS (245) + zinc 14 days. Trachoma = SAFE.

**Unit 5 — Programmes**

- **NTEP:** Detect–Treat–Prevent–Build; Ni-kshay; Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana.
- **NVBDCP:** malaria, dengue, chikungunya, filariasis, JE, kala-azar.
- **NACP (NACO):** ICTC, PPTCT, ART centres, targeted interventions.
- **UIP + Mission Indradhanush**; **NLEP** (MDT); **NP-NCD** (screen 30+ for BP, diabetes, cancers); **NMHP** (DMHP); **NTCP** (COTPA); **NIDDCP**; **Anemia Mukt Bharat**; **NPCBVI**; **IDSP**.
- **Ayushman Bharat** = Ayushman Arogya Mandirs + PM-JAY; **Jan Aushadhi** = generics.

**Unit 6 — Pharmacoeconomics**

| Analysis | Outcome unit | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CMA | Equal outcomes | Pick the cheaper |
| CEA | Clinical units; ICER | Same type of outcome |
| CBA | Money; benefit-cost ratio | Different outcomes |
| CUA | QALY | Quality of life matters |

Costs = direct medical, direct non-medical, indirect, intangible. Outcomes = ECHO. QALY = years × utility.

**Role of pharmacist (write in every long answer):** educate, counsel, screen and refer, supply preventive products, support national programmes, report ADRs and cases, promote rational use and generics, safe disposal.

# National immunization schedule (children and adults)

**Aim:** To prepare a chart of the National Immunization Schedule for children and pregnant women, an adult vaccine schedule, and a list of vaccines not included in the national programme.

> This is a chart and counselling activity. India updates its schedule from time to time; check your chart against the latest MoHFW immunisation card before display.

## Principle

Vaccines give active artificial immunity. Doses must be given at the right age and interval for full protection. The Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) gives these vaccines free. A pharmacist uses the schedule to remind parents of due doses and to advise adults on vaccines they need.

## Requirements

Chart paper, coloured pens or a computer, the current MoHFW immunisation card, sample empty vaccine vials or pictures, a model vaccine carrier with ice packs.

## Procedure

1. Draw a table with columns: Age – Vaccine – Dose – Route – Site.
2. Fill the childhood schedule (below), using one colour for each disease group.
3. Add the pregnant-women row (Td).
4. Make a second chart for adults and for vaccines outside the UIP.
5. Add a box on cold chain (+2 to +8 °C, VVM) and common minor side effects.
6. Role play: one student is a mother with a 10-week-old baby; another, as pharmacist, explains the due vaccines and the next visit.

## Observations — chart content

**Children (UIP)**

| Age | Vaccines |
| --- | --- |
| At birth | BCG, OPV-0, Hepatitis B birth dose (within 24 hours) |
| 6 weeks | OPV-1, Pentavalent-1, Rotavirus-1, fIPV-1, PCV-1 |
| 10 weeks | OPV-2, Pentavalent-2, Rotavirus-2 |
| 14 weeks | OPV-3, Pentavalent-3, Rotavirus-3, fIPV-2, PCV-2 |
| 9–12 months | MR-1, JE-1 (endemic districts), PCV booster, Vitamin A (1st dose) |
| 16–24 months | MR-2, JE-2, DPT booster-1, OPV booster, Vitamin A (2nd dose, then every 6 months till 5 years) |
| 5–6 years | DPT booster-2 |
| 10 years and 16 years | Td |
| Pregnant women | Td-1 early in pregnancy, Td-2 four weeks later (or one Td booster if vaccinated in the last 3 years) |

Pentavalent = DPT + Hepatitis B + Hib. Routes: BCG intradermal (left upper arm); OPV and rotavirus oral; pentavalent, PCV, Td intramuscular (thigh in infants); MR subcutaneous; fIPV intradermal.

**Adults (advised, mostly outside UIP):** Td booster every 10 years and after dirty wounds; yearly influenza vaccine for those over 60, chronic patients, health workers and pregnant women; hepatitis B (health workers, high-risk groups); pneumococcal vaccine for elderly and chronic patients; rabies pre-exposure for vets and animal handlers.

**Vaccines not in the national programme (examples):** varicella, hepatitis A, typhoid conjugate, MMR (UIP gives MR), influenza, meningococcal, HPV (being introduced for adolescent girls — check the current status), cholera, herpes zoster, rabies pre-exposure.

## Result

A chart of the national immunization schedule, adult vaccines and non-UIP vaccines was prepared and used for a counselling role play.

## Precautions

- Use only the current official schedule; note the date of the source.
- Never advise skipping doses; a missed dose is given at the next visit without restarting.
- Live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency.

## Viva questions

1. **What does pentavalent vaccine protect against?** Diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B and Hib.
2. **Which vaccines are given at birth?** BCG, OPV-0 and hepatitis B birth dose.
3. **Why is MR given twice?** The second dose catches children who did not respond to the first and raises protection.
4. **What is Mission Indradhanush?** A catch-up drive to vaccinate children and pregnant women who missed doses.
5. **Which vaccine is given to pregnant women?** Td (tetanus–diphtheria), two doses or one booster.
6. **What is a VVM?** Vaccine vial monitor; shows whether the vial has had too much heat.
practicals.title: National immunization schedule: children, adults, non-UIP vaccines

# Reproductive and child health (RCH): nutritional aspects and national programmes

**Aim:** To study the nutritional aspects of reproductive and child health and the related national programmes, and to prepare a chart or presentation for community education.

## Principle

The health of a child depends on the mother's nutrition before and during pregnancy, breastfeeding, and the child's diet in the first years ("first 1000 days"). The RCH approach, now part of RMNCH+A under NHM, covers adolescents, pregnant and lactating women, newborns and children with services including nutrition supplements.

## Requirements

Chart paper or slides, sample IFA tablets and syrup (or pictures), ORS and zinc packets, a growth chart (from the Mother and Child Protection card), MUAC tape.

## Procedure

1. Divide into groups: adolescent girls, pregnant women, lactating mothers, infants (0–6 months), young children (6 months–5 years).
2. For each group list the main nutritional needs, common deficiencies and the government service that addresses them.
3. Prepare a chart linking each service to its programme.
4. Demonstrate a growth chart entry and MUAC measurement on a doll or volunteer.
5. Role play counselling of a pregnant woman on IFA and diet.

## Observations — chart content

| Group | Needs / problems | Services and programmes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adolescents | Anaemia, early marriage | Weekly IFA (Anemia Mukt Bharat / RKSK), deworming, nutrition education, menstrual hygiene |
| Pregnant women | Extra energy, protein, iron, folic acid, calcium | Daily IFA from second trimester, calcium, Td, ANC (PMSMA), take-home ration from Anganwadi, JSY/JSSK |
| Lactating mothers | Extra energy and protein | Supplementary nutrition (ICDS), counselling on breastfeeding |
| Infants 0–6 months | Breast milk only | Early and exclusive breastfeeding, home-based newborn care by ASHA |
| Children 6 months–5 years | Complementary feeding, growth | Anganwadi supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, IFA syrup, vitamin A, deworming, ORS + zinc, immunisation |
| School children | Nutrition, worms | PM POSHAN (mid-day meal), National Deworming Day, RBSK screening |

**Complementary feeding tips (from 6 months):** start with thick mashed foods (dal-rice, khichdi, mashed banana), add a little oil or ghee, increase frequency and variety with age, continue breastfeeding.

## Result

The nutritional needs at each stage of the RCH life cycle and the programmes that meet them were studied and presented as a chart.

## Precautions

- Give only current government guidance on doses of IFA and vitamin A; check with the programme guidelines.
- Use simple local-language messages; respect privacy when counselling.

## Viva questions

1. **What does RMNCH+A stand for?** Reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health.
2. **When should breastfeeding begin?** Within one hour of birth.
3. **What is ICDS?** Integrated Child Development Services, delivered through Anganwadi centres (supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, pre-school education).
4. **Why give IFA in pregnancy?** To prevent maternal anaemia and low birth weight; folic acid prevents neural tube defects.
5. **What is MUAC?** Mid-upper arm circumference; a quick screen for acute malnutrition in children.
practicals.title: Reproductive and child health: nutritional aspects and programmes

# Family planning devices

**Aim:** To identify and study family planning devices and contraceptives, and to counsel a couple on choosing a method.

## Principle

Contraceptives prevent pregnancy by blocking sperm (barrier), preventing ovulation (hormonal), preventing fertilisation or implantation (IUD, centchroman), or by permanent closure of the vas or tubes. The pharmacist explains use, side effects and what to do when a dose is missed.

## Requirements

Demonstration samples or pictures: male and female condom, diaphragm, Cu-T 380A and Cu-T 375 (demonstration pieces), combined oral pill pack, centchroman tablets, DMPA injection vial, emergency contraceptive pill, a pelvic model, chart paper.

## Procedure

1. Display each device and label it with its name, type and mode of action.
2. Prepare a chart table of the methods (below).
3. Demonstrate correct use of a male condom on a model (check expiry, open carefully, pinch tip, roll on, remove and dispose in a dustbin).
4. Show how a 28-day pill pack is followed (21 hormone tablets + 7 iron tablets) and explain missed-pill advice as per the leaflet.
5. Role play counselling of a newly married couple and of a mother with a 3-month-old baby.

## Observations

| Method | Type | Action | Duration / use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Male condom | Barrier | Stops sperm entry; also prevents STDs/HIV | Each act |
| Diaphragm | Barrier | Covers cervix, used with spermicide | Each act |
| Cu-T 380A | IUD | Copper toxic to sperm, prevents implantation | About 10 years |
| Cu-T 375 | IUD | As above | About 5 years |
| Combined oral pill (Mala-N) | Hormonal | Stops ovulation | One tablet daily |
| Centchroman (Chhaya) | Non-hormonal pill | Prevents implantation | Twice weekly for 3 months, then weekly |
| DMPA (Antara) | Injectable progestin | Stops ovulation | Every 3 months |
| Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg | Emergency pill | Delays ovulation | Within 72 hours; not regular use |
| Vasectomy / tubectomy | Permanent | Blocks vas / tubes | Permanent |

## Result

Family planning devices were identified, their mode of action and use were studied, and counselling was practised.

## Precautions

- Maintain privacy and a non-judgemental attitude.
- Check expiry dates; store condoms away from heat.
- Combined pills are not advised for breastfeeding mothers in the first months, smokers over 35, or women with a history of clots; refer such women.
- IUD insertion and sterilisation are done only by trained providers.

## Viva questions

1. **Which method also protects against STDs?** The condom.
2. **How long is Cu-T 380A effective?** About 10 years.
3. **What is LAM?** Lactational amenorrhoea method — natural contraception with exclusive breastfeeding, baby under 6 months, no periods.
4. **When should an emergency pill be taken?** As early as possible, within 72 hours of unprotected sex.
5. **Which is the simpler permanent method?** Vasectomy (no-scalpel), done for the male partner.
practicals.title: Family planning devices

# Microscopical observation of microbes (ready-made slides)

**Aim:** To observe and identify different micro-organisms using ready-made stained slides under the compound microscope.

## Principle

Microbes are too small to see with the eye. A compound microscope with the oil-immersion objective (100×) and a 10× eyepiece magnifies 1000 times. Stains make cells visible: in the **Gram stain**, Gram-positive bacteria keep crystal violet and look purple; Gram-negative bacteria lose it and take the pink counter-stain (safranin). In the **Ziehl–Neelsen (acid-fast)** stain, mycobacteria hold carbol fuchsin and look red on a blue background.

## Requirements

Compound microscope, cedar wood or immersion oil, lens paper, xylene (for cleaning), ready-made slides: Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, E. coli, Bacillus, M. tuberculosis (ZN), yeast (Candida), a mould (Aspergillus/Penicillium), malaria parasite in blood smear, helminth egg (Ascaris).

## Procedure

1. Place the microscope on a firm table; switch on the light and centre the slide on the stage.
2. Focus first with the low-power (10×) objective using the coarse knob.
3. Move to high power (40×) and refine with the fine knob.
4. For bacteria, put a drop of immersion oil on the slide and turn the 100× objective into the oil; focus with the fine knob only.
5. Observe shape, arrangement and colour; draw what you see in a circle.
6. After use, wipe oil from the objective with lens paper, lower the stage and switch off.

## Observations

| Slide | What is seen | Identification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staphylococcus | Purple round cells in grape-like clusters | Gram-positive cocci in clusters |
| Streptococcus | Purple round cells in chains | Gram-positive cocci in chains |
| E. coli | Pink short rods, scattered | Gram-negative bacilli |
| Bacillus | Purple large rods, often in chains | Gram-positive bacilli |
| M. tuberculosis (ZN) | Thin red rods on a blue background | Acid-fast bacilli |
| Candida | Oval budding cells (purple) | Yeast |
| Aspergillus | Branched threads with spore heads | Mould (fungus) |
| Malaria smear | Ring forms inside red blood cells | Plasmodium |
| Ascaris egg | Oval egg with thick, bumpy shell | Roundworm egg |

Total magnification = objective × eyepiece (e.g. 100 × 10 = 1000×).

## Result

Different micro-organisms were observed and identified from ready-made slides as recorded above.

## Precautions

- Use oil only with the 100× objective; clean it after use.
- Never lower the objective while looking through the eyepiece (it can break the slide).
- Handle slides by the edges; return them to the box.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the total magnification with oil immersion?** About 1000× (100× objective × 10× eyepiece).
2. **Why do Gram-positive bacteria stay purple?** Their thick peptidoglycan wall holds the crystal violet–iodine complex.
3. **Which organisms are acid-fast?** Mycobacteria (TB and leprosy bacilli).
4. **Why is oil used?** It has nearly the same refractive index as glass, so less light is lost and the image is clearer.
5. **Name a disease caused by a yeast.** Oral thrush (Candida).
practicals.title: Microscopical observation of microbes (ready-made slides)

# Oral health and hygiene

**Aim:** To demonstrate correct oral hygiene practices and prepare awareness material on oral diseases and their prevention.

## Principle

Dental plaque — a sticky film of bacteria on teeth — turns sugars into acid that dissolves enamel (**dental caries**) and irritates gums (**gingivitis**, which can progress to **periodontitis** and tooth loss). Regular brushing with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between teeth and limiting sugary snacks remove plaque and strengthen enamel. Tobacco and areca nut cause oral cancer and pre-cancerous patches.

## Requirements

Tooth model or large jaw model, soft-bristled toothbrush, fluoride toothpaste, dental floss, tongue cleaner, disclosing tablets (optional), mirror, chart paper with pictures of caries, gingivitis, oral thrush and leukoplakia.

## Procedure

1. Show a healthy tooth and a decayed tooth on a chart; explain how plaque forms.
2. Demonstrate brushing on the model: pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste; brush at a 45° angle to the gum line with gentle short strokes; clean outer, inner and chewing surfaces; about 2 minutes; twice a day (morning and before bed).
3. Demonstrate flossing between teeth and cleaning of the tongue.
4. (Optional) Chew a disclosing tablet to colour plaque, then brush and see the difference.
5. Prepare an awareness poster: "Brush twice, floss once, cut down sugar, quit tobacco, see a dentist yearly."
6. Role play counselling for a child with tooth decay and an adult chewing gutkha.

## Observations

| Practice | Correct method | Benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brushing | Twice daily, 2 minutes, soft brush, fluoride paste | Removes plaque, prevents caries |
| Toothbrush | Change every 3 months or when bristles fray | Effective cleaning |
| Flossing | Once daily | Cleans between teeth |
| Diet | Fewer sticky and sugary snacks between meals; rinse after sweets | Less acid attack |
| Tobacco/areca nut | Avoid | Prevents oral cancer and gum disease |
| Dental check-up | At least once a year | Early detection |

**Common oral problems:** dental caries, gingivitis, periodontitis, bad breath, oral ulcers, oral thrush, dental fluorosis (excess fluoride in water), oral cancer.

## Result

Correct brushing and flossing were demonstrated and awareness material on oral hygiene was prepared.

## Precautions

- Use only a pea-sized amount of toothpaste for children and supervise to avoid swallowing.
- Avoid hard brushes and very hard brushing, which wear gums.
- Refer any non-healing ulcer or white/red patch in the mouth to a dentist.

## Viva questions

1. **What is dental plaque?** A sticky film of bacteria and food residue on teeth.
2. **How does fluoride protect teeth?** It strengthens enamel and helps repair early decay.
3. **What is gingivitis?** Inflammation of the gums, with bleeding on brushing.
4. **Name two habits causing oral cancer.** Chewing tobacco/gutkha and smoking (also areca nut, alcohol).
5. **How often should a toothbrush be changed?** About every 3 months.
practicals.title: Oral health and hygiene

# Personal hygiene and etiquette: hand-washing, cough and sneeze etiquette

**Aim:** To demonstrate correct hand-washing and hand-rub technique, and cough and sneeze etiquette.

## Principle

Hands carry microbes from faeces, surfaces and respiratory secretions to the mouth, eyes and other people. Washing with soap and water removes dirt and microbes; alcohol-based hand rub (60–80% alcohol) kills many microbes when hands are not visibly dirty. Covering coughs and sneezes stops droplets that spread influenza, COVID-19, TB and colds.

## Requirements

Wash basin with running water, plain soap, alcohol-based hand rub, disposable paper towels, a fluorescent lotion and UV lamp (optional) or a coloured paint to show missed areas, tissues, a covered dustbin, chart showing the WHO hand-wash steps.

## Procedure — hand-washing with soap and water (about 40–60 seconds)

1. Wet hands with clean running water and apply enough soap.
2. Rub palm to palm.
3. Right palm over the back of the left hand with fingers interlaced, and vice versa.
4. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
5. Backs of fingers against the opposite palm with fingers interlocked.
6. Rotational rubbing of each thumb clasped in the other palm.
7. Rotational rubbing of the fingertips in the opposite palm (cleans nails), and wrists.
8. Rinse well, dry with a single-use towel, and use the towel to turn off the tap.

**Hand rub:** apply a palmful, follow steps 2–7 until hands are dry (about 20–30 seconds).

**Cough and sneeze etiquette**

1. Cover mouth and nose with a tissue; throw the tissue in a closed bin at once.
2. If no tissue, cough or sneeze into the bent elbow, not the hands.
3. Clean hands afterwards.
4. Wear a mask when sick with cough or cold; keep distance from others; stay home if unwell.

## Observations

| Step | Area cleaned | Done correctly (✓/✗) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Palm to palm | Palms | |
| Back of hands | Dorsum | |
| Interlaced fingers | Finger webs | |
| Backs of fingers | Knuckles | |
| Thumbs | Thumbs | |
| Fingertips | Nails | |

Commonly missed areas (seen with paint or UV lotion): thumbs, fingertips, backs of hands, wrists.

**Five key moments for hand-washing at home:** before eating, before preparing food, before feeding a child, after using the toilet, after cleaning a child or touching waste. In health care, WHO lists five moments: before touching a patient, before a clean/aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure, after touching a patient, after touching patient surroundings.

## Result

Correct hand-washing, hand-rub and cough/sneeze etiquette were demonstrated and practised.

## Precautions

- Remove rings and watches; keep nails short.
- Use soap and water (not rub) when hands are visibly dirty.
- Do not touch the face with unwashed hands.

## Viva questions

1. **How long should hand-washing take?** About 40–60 seconds (hand rub 20–30 seconds).
2. **Which diseases does hand-washing prevent?** Diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, worm infections, respiratory infections.
3. **When should soap and water be used instead of hand rub?** When hands are visibly soiled.
4. **Where should you sneeze if you have no tissue?** Into the bent elbow.
5. **Which areas are most often missed?** Thumbs, fingertips and backs of hands.
practicals.title: Hand-washing technique and cough and sneeze etiquette

# Types of masks and PPE: wearing, removing and disposal

**Aim:** To identify different types of masks and personal protective equipment (PPE) and to demonstrate correct donning, doffing and disposal.

## Principle

PPE forms a barrier between the wearer and infectious material. A **cloth mask** reduces spread of droplets from the wearer; a **surgical (3-ply) mask** protects against droplets and splashes; an **N95 respirator** filters at least 95% of very small airborne particles when it fits tightly. Wrong removal can contaminate the wearer, so the order of putting on and taking off matters.

## Requirements

Cloth mask, 3-ply surgical mask, N95 respirator, face shield, goggles, gown or coverall, gloves, cap and shoe covers, hand rub, yellow and red bio-medical waste bags.

## Procedure

**Wearing a surgical mask:** clean hands → check sides (coloured side out, metal strip on top) → place over nose and mouth → fix ear loops or ties → press the metal strip on the nose → do not touch the front while wearing → change when wet.

**N95 fit:** hold the respirator, place it under the chin, pull straps over the head, mould the nose clip with both hands, and do a seal check (breathe out — no air should leak at the edges).

**Donning sequence (full PPE):**

1. Hand hygiene
2. Gown/coverall
3. Mask or respirator
4. Goggles or face shield
5. Gloves (over the gown cuffs)

**Doffing sequence:**

1. Gloves (glove-in-glove technique)
2. Goggles or face shield (hold by the strap)
3. Gown (roll inside-out, away from the body)
4. Mask or respirator (by the straps, without touching the front)
5. Hand hygiene (also between steps if hands get contaminated)

**Disposal:** used masks, gloves and gowns from patient care go into the bio-medical waste stream as per the hospital's colour coding; at home, used masks are wrapped in paper and put in a closed dustbin.

## Observations

| Type | Protects against | Reusable? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloth mask | Wearer's droplets (source control) | Yes, after washing |
| Surgical 3-ply mask | Droplets and splashes | No |
| N95 respirator | Airborne particles (TB, aerosols) | No (single use in routine care) |
| Face shield / goggles | Splashes to eyes and face | Reusable after disinfection |
| Gown/coverall | Body contamination | Disposable or washable types |
| Gloves | Hand contamination | No |

## Result

Different masks and PPE were identified, and correct donning, doffing and disposal were demonstrated.

## Precautions

- Clean hands before wearing and after removing PPE.
- Never pull a mask under the chin and back again; never reuse disposable masks.
- Beards prevent an N95 from sealing.

## Viva questions

1. **What does "N95" mean?** Filters at least 95% of airborne particles when properly fitted.
2. **Which item is removed first?** Gloves.
3. **Which item is removed last?** The mask or respirator, followed by hand hygiene.
4. **What is a seal check?** Breathing out after wearing an N95 to feel for leaks at the edges.
5. **What is the main use of a cloth mask?** To reduce spread of droplets from the wearer.
practicals.title: Masks and PPE: wearing, removing and disposal

# Menstrual hygiene and products used

**Aim:** To study menstrual hygiene practices and products, and to prepare counselling and awareness material.

## Principle

Menstruation is a normal monthly process. Poor menstrual hygiene can cause genital and urinary infections, skin rashes and school absence; myths and stigma stop girls from asking for help. Safe, clean absorbent products, regular changing, washing and proper disposal keep girls and women healthy.

## Requirements

Samples or pictures of disposable sanitary pads, reusable cloth pads, tampons, menstrual cup, period underwear; a chart; a model of the female reproductive system; paper bags for disposal.

## Procedure

1. Explain the menstrual cycle in simple words (about 28 days; bleeding about 3–7 days).
2. Display each product and explain how it is used, how often it is changed and how it is cleaned or disposed of.
3. Prepare a chart of good practices and common myths.
4. Role play: a pharmacist counselling a 13-year-old girl about her first period, and a woman asking about a menstrual cup.
5. Mention government schemes: menstrual hygiene under RKSK, low-cost sanitary napkins at Jan Aushadhi Kendras.

## Observations

| Product | Use | Change / care | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Disposable sanitary pad | External, sticks to underwear | Every 4–6 hours | Wrap and put in a covered bin or incinerator |
| Reusable cloth pad | External | Wash with soap and cold water, dry in sunlight | Low cost, eco-friendly |
| Tampon | Inserted in vagina | Every 4–8 hours; use lowest absorbency needed | Rare toxic shock syndrome if left too long |
| Menstrual cup (medical-grade silicone) | Inserted, collects blood | Empty every 8–12 hours; boil between cycles | Reusable for years |
| Period underwear | Absorbent layer | Wash after use | Light flow or backup |

**Good practices:** bathe daily, wash the genital area front-to-back with plain water, change products regularly, wash hands before and after, keep a spare pad, eat iron-rich food.

**Myths to correct:** "Do not bathe or exercise during periods", "girls are impure", "do not enter the kitchen" — none has a health basis.

**When to see a doctor:** very heavy bleeding, periods lasting more than 7 days, severe pain, no periods by age 15, foul-smelling discharge, itching.

## Result

Menstrual hygiene practices and products were studied, and counselling material was prepared.

## Precautions

- Respect privacy and speak sensitively.
- Never flush pads or tampons; they block drains.
- Do not reuse cloth that is damp or not sun-dried.

## Viva questions

1. **How often should a sanitary pad be changed?** About every 4–6 hours.
2. **What is toxic shock syndrome?** A rare, serious bacterial toxin illness linked to leaving tampons in too long.
3. **How is a menstrual cup cleaned?** Rinsed when emptied and boiled between cycles.
4. **Where can low-cost sanitary napkins be bought?** At Jan Aushadhi Kendras.
5. **Why dry cloth pads in sunlight?** Sunlight helps kill microbes and dries them fully.
practicals.title: Menstrual hygiene and products used

# First aid and Basic Life Support (CPR, AED, choking)

**Aim:** To learn the basics of first aid and to practise Basic Life Support (BLS) — recognising sudden cardiac arrest, giving CPR, using an AED, and relieving foreign-body airway obstruction (choking).

> Practise only on a manikin. Follow the current resuscitation guidelines taught by your instructor; techniques are updated from time to time.

## Principle

**First aid** is the immediate care given to an injured or suddenly ill person before medical help arrives — to preserve life, prevent the condition from getting worse, and promote recovery.

In **sudden cardiac arrest (SCA)** the heart stops pumping; the brain starts to be damaged within minutes. **Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR)** — chest compressions with or without rescue breaths — keeps blood flowing to the brain and heart. An **automated external defibrillator (AED)** gives an electric shock that can restore a normal rhythm. Early CPR and early defibrillation greatly improve survival (the "chain of survival").

## Requirements

Adult and infant CPR manikins, AED trainer, pocket mask, gloves, first-aid box, audio-visual material.

## Procedure — adult BLS

1. **Scene safety:** make sure the area is safe for you and the victim.
2. **Check response:** tap the shoulders and shout "Are you all right?"
3. **Call for help:** shout for help; ask someone to call the ambulance (108 or 112) and bring an AED.
4. **Check breathing** for no more than 10 seconds (no breathing or only gasping = cardiac arrest).
5. **Start chest compressions:** heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), other hand on top, arms straight; push hard and fast — depth about 5–6 cm, rate 100–120 per minute; allow the chest to rise fully between compressions; minimise pauses.
6. **Rescue breaths (if trained):** open the airway by head tilt–chin lift, give 2 breaths, each over about 1 second, watching the chest rise. Ratio **30 compressions : 2 breaths**. Untrained rescuers may give compressions only (hands-only CPR).
7. **AED:** switch on and follow voice prompts; stick pads (upper right chest, lower left side); make sure no one touches the victim during analysis and shock; resume CPR immediately after the shock.
8. Continue until the victim breathes normally, help arrives, or you are exhausted.

**Children and infants:** compression depth about one-third of the chest (about 5 cm in children, about 4 cm in infants; two fingers or two thumbs for infants); single rescuer 30:2, two trained rescuers 15:2.

**Choking (FBAO):**

- Conscious adult who cannot speak or cough effectively: give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre); repeat.
- Infant: 5 back blows face-down on your forearm, then 5 chest thrusts; no abdominal thrusts.
- If the person becomes unconscious: start CPR.

## Observations

| Item | Standard | Achieved on manikin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compression rate | 100–120/min | |
| Compression depth (adult) | 5–6 cm | |
| Ratio (single rescuer) | 30:2 | |
| Time to first compression | As short as possible | |
| AED pad position | Upper right chest, lower left side | |

## Result

The basics of first aid were learnt, and adult and infant CPR, AED use and choking relief were practised on manikins.

## Precautions

- Ensure your own safety first; wear gloves when possible.
- Do not stop CPR to check the pulse repeatedly.
- No one should touch the victim while the AED analyses or shocks.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the compression-to-breath ratio for an adult?** 30:2.
2. **What is the rate of chest compressions?** 100–120 per minute.
3. **What does an AED do?** Analyses the heart rhythm and gives a shock if it is shockable.
4. **What is the Heimlich manoeuvre?** Abdominal thrusts to expel an object blocking the airway.
5. **What is hands-only CPR?** Continuous chest compressions without rescue breaths, for untrained bystanders.
practicals.title: First aid and Basic Life Support (CPR, AED, choking)

# First aid in medical emergencies: snake bite, dog bite, insecticide poisoning, fractures, burns, epilepsy

**Aim:** To learn and demonstrate first-aid and emergency measures for common medical emergencies.

## Principle

Correct first aid in the first minutes reduces harm and buys time to reach hospital. Many harmful traditional practices (tourniquets, cutting, applying toothpaste on burns) make things worse; the pharmacist must replace them with correct advice.

## Requirements

First-aid box, bandages, triangular sling, splints (or cardboard/rolled newspaper), clean cloth, cling film, soap and water, povidone-iodine, gloves, charts, role-play cards.

## Procedure and observations

| Emergency | Do | Do not | Definitive care |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Snake bite** | Reassure; keep the person still; immobilise the bitten limb like a fracture; remove rings, watch, tight clothing; carry to hospital quickly; note time and the snake's appearance if safe | Tourniquet, cutting, sucking, ice, herbal remedies, trying to catch the snake | Polyvalent anti-snake venom (covers cobra, krait, Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper) in hospital |
| **Dog (animal) bite** | Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes; apply povidone-iodine or alcohol; go to a health centre the same day | Chilli, oil, turmeric on the wound; early stitching | Anti-rabies vaccine as per category; rabies immunoglobulin for deep (category III) bites; tetanus cover |
| **Insecticide (organophosphate) poisoning** | Remove from exposure; remove contaminated clothes; wash skin with soap and water; keep airway clear, recovery position if drowsy; take the container to hospital | Inducing vomiting; giving milk or oil | Atropine and pralidoxime in hospital; observe for breathing failure |
| **Fracture** | Stop bleeding; immobilise the joint above and below with a splint; support an arm in a sling; check circulation below the splint | Trying to straighten the bone; moving a suspected spine injury | X-ray, reduction, plaster or surgery |
| **Burns** | Cool under clean running tap water for about 20 minutes; remove rings and loose clothing (not stuck cloth); cover loosely with cling film or a clean cloth; give fluids if conscious | Ice, butter, toothpaste, oil; bursting blisters | Hospital for large, deep, face, hand, genital or electrical burns; area by the "rule of nines" |
| **Epileptic seizure** | Stay calm; protect the head with something soft; move hard objects away; loosen tight clothing; time the seizure; after it stops, turn into recovery position | Putting anything in the mouth; holding the person down; giving water during the fit | Call emergency if the fit lasts over 5 minutes, repeats, or occurs in water or pregnancy |

**Rule of nines (adult):** head and neck 9%, each arm 9%, front of trunk 18%, back of trunk 18%, each leg 18%, genitals 1%.

**Recovery position:** person on their side, top knee bent, head tilted back to keep the airway open — used for an unconscious person who is breathing.

## Result

First-aid steps for snake bite, dog bite, insecticide poisoning, fractures, burns and epilepsy were learnt and demonstrated through role plays.

## Precautions

- Protect yourself (gloves, avoid contact with poison).
- Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious person.
- Always arrange transport to a health facility after first aid.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is a tourniquet not used in snake bite?** It can cause gangrene and does not stop venom effectively.
2. **What is the first step after a dog bite?** Wash the wound with soap and running water for about 15 minutes.
3. **What is the antidote treatment for organophosphate poisoning?** Atropine and pralidoxime (in hospital).
4. **How long should a burn be cooled?** About 20 minutes under running water.
5. **What should not be done during a seizure?** Put anything in the mouth or hold the person down.
practicals.title: Emergency first aid: snake bite, dog bite, poisoning, fractures, burns, epilepsy

# Role of the pharmacist in disaster management

**Aim:** To study the disaster management cycle and the role of the pharmacist in preparedness and response, through a chart or case study.

## Principle

A **disaster** is a serious disruption of a community's functioning, causing loss of life, property or environment, beyond the community's ability to cope with its own resources. Disasters may be natural (earthquake, flood, landslide, cloudburst, cyclone, epidemic) or man-made (fire, industrial gas leak, road and rail accidents, war). Himachal Pradesh is prone to earthquakes, landslides, flash floods and cloudbursts.

India's **Disaster Management Act, 2005** set up the **National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA)** headed by the Prime Minister, State Disaster Management Authorities, District authorities and the **National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)**.

## Requirements

Chart paper, maps of the district, a sample emergency drug kit list, newspaper reports of a recent disaster, the district disaster management plan (if available).

## Procedure

1. Draw the disaster management cycle (below).
2. List the medicines and supplies needed after a flood or earthquake.
3. Study one recent disaster from newspapers and write what health problems arose.
4. Prepare a table of pharmacist roles in each phase.
5. Hold a mock drill: set up a dispensing point in a relief camp and prioritise patients.

```text
        PREPAREDNESS  --->  RESPONSE
             ^                  |
             |                  v
        MITIGATION  <---   RECOVERY
   (the cycle repeats; prevention and mitigation reduce future harm)
```

## Observations

| Phase | Pharmacist's role |
| --- | --- |
| Mitigation and preparedness | Prepare emergency drug kits and a stock list; maintain buffer stocks and a cold-chain backup; train staff and volunteers in first aid; plan alternative supply routes; keep a list of patients on essential long-term drugs (insulin, ART, TB, dialysis) |
| Response | Dispense and manage donated medicines; supply ORS, antibiotics, analgesics, tetanus vaccine, chlorine tablets; maintain cold chain; prevent outbreaks (water purification, hygiene advice); give first aid and counselling; keep records |
| Recovery | Restore supply chains; continue care of chronic patients; dispose of expired or unusable donated drugs safely; support mental health referrals; review and update the plan |

**Common health problems after floods:** diarrhoea and cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E, leptospirosis, skin and eye infections, malaria and dengue, snake bites, injuries.

**Essential relief items:** ORS, zinc, paracetamol, antibiotics as per protocol, antiseptics, dressings, tetanus vaccine, chlorine tablets/bleaching powder, insulin and chronic medicines, sanitary pads, mosquito nets.

## Result

The disaster management cycle and the role of the pharmacist in each phase were studied and presented.

## Precautions

- Accept donated medicines only if needed, labelled, in date and in a known language.
- Keep records of all medicines received and dispensed.
- Follow instructions of the incident command system.

## Viva questions

1. **Define disaster.** A serious disruption of a community causing losses beyond its capacity to cope with its own resources.
2. **Which Act governs disaster management in India?** The Disaster Management Act, 2005.
3. **Name the four phases of the disaster cycle.** Mitigation, preparedness, response, recovery.
4. **Which diseases rise after floods?** Diarrhoeal diseases, typhoid, hepatitis A/E, leptospirosis, malaria, dengue.
5. **What is NDRF?** National Disaster Response Force — a specialised force for disaster response.
practicals.title: Role of the pharmacist in disaster management

# Marketed disinfectants, antiseptics, fumigating agents, antilarval agents and repellents

**Aim:** To study marketed preparations of disinfectants, antiseptics, fumigating agents, antilarval agents and mosquito repellents, noting their active ingredients, uses and precautions.

## Principle

- **Disinfectant:** a chemical that kills or removes harmful microbes on **non-living** surfaces and objects (floors, instruments).
- **Antiseptic:** a chemical safe enough to apply to **living** tissue (skin, wounds) to reduce microbes.
- **Sterilisation:** killing all forms of life including spores (autoclave, not chemicals at routine strength).
- **Fumigation:** disinfection of a closed room with a gas or vapour.
- **Antilarval agent (larvicide):** kills mosquito larvae in water.
- **Repellent:** keeps insects away from the skin or a room.

## Requirements

Labels or packs of marketed products (collect from local shops/pharmacy), chart paper.

## Procedure

1. Collect at least two products of each type.
2. Read each label and note: active ingredient and strength, category, directions, dilution, precautions, storage.
3. Prepare a table and a chart.
4. Prepare a 1 in 20 dilution of a disinfectant concentrate as instructed by the teacher (e.g. 5 ml made up to 100 ml) and label it.

## Observations

| Category | Active ingredient (examples) | Uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phenolic disinfectants | Cresol (as soap solution), phenol | Floors, drains, toilets |
| Chloroxylenol antiseptic | Chloroxylenol (PCMX) solution | Skin, cuts, bath water, general household |
| Chlorhexidine + cetrimide | Chlorhexidine gluconate with cetrimide | Wound cleaning, skin, surgical scrub |
| Iodophor | Povidone-iodine 5–10% | Wounds, pre-operative skin, dog bites |
| Alcohols | Ethanol or isopropyl alcohol 60–80% | Hand rub, skin before injection |
| Chlorine compounds | Sodium hypochlorite, bleaching powder | Surfaces, blood spills, water disinfection |
| Hydrogen peroxide | 3% (about 10 volume) solution | Wound cleaning |
| Aldehydes | Glutaraldehyde 2%, formaldehyde | Instrument disinfection; formaldehyde for fumigation |
| Quaternary ammonium | Benzalkonium chloride | Antiseptic, surface cleaner, preservative |
| Fumigating agents | Formaldehyde vapour (formalin with potassium permanganate), hydrogen peroxide vapour | Operation theatres, isolation rooms |
| Antilarval agents | Temephos, Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti), larvivorous fish (Gambusia, guppy), mineral oil | Water tanks, ponds, drains |
| Repellents | DEET, picaridin, citronella oil creams; allethrin/transfluthrin coils and vaporisers; permethrin-treated nets | Personal protection, rooms |

## Result

The active ingredients, uses and precautions of marketed disinfectants, antiseptics, fumigants, larvicides and repellents were studied and tabulated.

## Precautions

- Never mix bleach with acids or ammonia-containing cleaners (toxic gases).
- Use the dilution on the label; strong solutions damage skin.
- Keep products away from children; repellents are not applied on wounds or near eyes.
- Ventilate rooms well after using coils and vaporisers; fumigated rooms are entered only after the vapour is cleared.

## Viva questions

1. **Difference between antiseptic and disinfectant?** Antiseptic is used on living tissue; disinfectant on non-living objects.
2. **Which concentration of alcohol is best as a hand rub?** About 60–80%.

4. **What is Gambusia?** A larvivorous fish that eats mosquito larvae.
5. **Name a common skin repellent.** DEET (N,N-diethyl-meta-toluamide).

# Health communication on communicable diseases (posters, podcasts, slides, short films)

**Aim:** To prepare health-communication material in a regional language on five communicable diseases — their signs, symptoms and prevention — for mass education.

## Principle

**Information, Education and Communication (IEC)** gives people knowledge; **behaviour change communication (BCC)** helps them adopt healthy practices. Good messages are simple, correct, in the local language, culturally acceptable, focused on one action, and repeated through many channels (posters, audio podcasts, videos, slides, social media, wall paintings, street plays).

## Requirements

Computer or smartphone with free editing apps, microphone, chart paper and colours, reference notes on the diseases, a local-language translator if needed.

## Procedure

1. Choose five diseases, for example dengue, tuberculosis, diarrhoea, COVID-19 and typhoid (or malaria, hepatitis, HIV).
2. For each disease write the key messages: what it is, how it spreads, warning signs, what to do, how to prevent it.
3. Choose the audience (school children, mothers, farmers, elderly) and the language (e.g. Hindi or the local dialect).
4. Prepare one product per disease: a poster, a 1–2 minute audio podcast, a 3–5 slide presentation, or a short video.
5. Pre-test the material with a few people and correct confusing parts.
6. Present to the class; collect feedback on clarity and accuracy.

## Observations — sample message plan

| Disease | Key message | Action asked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dengue | Day-biting mosquito breeds in clean stored water | Empty coolers and pots every week; use repellents; see a doctor for high fever |
| Tuberculosis | Cough for 2 weeks or more may be TB; treatment is free | Get sputum tested; complete the full course |
| Diarrhoea | Dehydration kills children | Give ORS and zinc; continue feeding; wash hands |
| COVID-19 / flu | Spreads by droplets and air | Cover coughs, wear a mask when ill, get vaccinated |
| Typhoid | Spreads through unsafe water and food | Drink boiled or chlorinated water; wash hands; eat hot food |

**Checklist for good material:** correct facts (checked against notes); one clear action; large readable text; local language; pictures over words; contact of nearest health centre or helpline.

## Result

Health-communication materials on five communicable diseases were prepared in a regional language and presented.

## Precautions

- Do not spread unverified claims or fear; avoid blaming or stigmatising patients.
- Use only images you have made or are free to use.
- Mention when to seek medical help.

## Viva questions

1. **What is IEC?** Information, Education and Communication — activities that give health knowledge to the public.
2. **What is BCC?** Behaviour change communication — messages aimed at changing a specific behaviour.
3. **Why use the regional language?** People understand and trust messages in their own language.
4. **What is pre-testing?** Trying material on a small group of the target audience before wide use.
5. **Name three channels for health messages.** Posters, radio/podcasts, videos (also street plays, social media).
practicals.title: Health communication on five communicable diseases

# Water purification: water testing kit and bleaching powder dose for wells and tanks

**Aim:** (a) To learn household water purification methods and use a water-testing kit; (b) to determine the available chlorine in bleaching powder; (c) to calculate the amount of bleaching powder needed to disinfect a well or tank.

## Principle

Chlorine kills most bacteria and viruses in water. **Bleaching powder** (chlorinated lime) contains about **33% available chlorine** when fresh, but loses strength on storage, so its strength should be checked. After chlorination, a **free residual chlorine of about 0.5 mg/L after 1 hour** shows that the dose was enough.

**Available chlorine (iodometry):** bleaching powder releases chlorine in acid; chlorine liberates iodine from potassium iodide; the iodine is titrated with sodium thiosulphate using starch.

Cl2 + 2KI → 2KCl + I2  I2 + 2Na2S2O3 → 2NaI + Na2S4O6

**Horrock's apparatus** finds the dose of bleaching powder for a well directly: a series of cups of well water receives increasing amounts of a bleaching powder solution; the first cup that turns blue with starch-iodide shows the number of level spoonfuls (2 g each) needed per 455 litres (100 gallons).

## Requirements

Bleaching powder, potassium iodide, glacial acetic acid, 0.1 N sodium thiosulphate, starch solution, conical flask, burette, mortar and pestle, volumetric flask; field water-testing kit (residual chlorine/orthotoluidine or DPD comparator, H2S bacterial strip test, pH strips); measuring tape for well dimensions; Horrock's apparatus if available.

## Procedure

**A. Available chlorine in bleaching powder**

1. Weigh about 2.5 g of bleaching powder (W), triturate with water and make up to 250 ml in a volumetric flask.
2. Pipette 25 ml into a conical flask, add about 1 g potassium iodide and 5 ml acetic acid (liberates iodine — brown colour).
3. Titrate with 0.1 N sodium thiosulphate till pale yellow; add starch (blue) and continue till colourless. Note volume V ml.

**B. Testing water with a kit**

1. Residual chlorine: add the reagent to the water sample and compare the colour with the standard (target about 0.5 mg/L).
2. Bacterial (H2S strip) test: add sample to the bottle, keep at room temperature 24–48 hours; black colour suggests faecal contamination.
3. pH: dip strip and compare.

**C. Dose for a well**

1. Measure the diameter (d) of the well and the depth of water (h) in metres.
2. Calculate the volume and the bleaching powder needed.

## Observations and calculations

**A. Available chlorine**

1 ml of 0.1 N sodium thiosulphate ≡ 0.003545 g of chlorine.

% available chlorine = (V × N × 35.45 × 250 × 100) ÷ (W × 1000 × 25)

*Worked example:* W = 2.5 g, V = 23.5 ml, N = 0.1 → (23.5 × 0.1 × 35.45 × 10 × 100) ÷ (2.5 × 1000) = **about 33.3%**.

**C. Well disinfection**

Volume of water (litres) = 3.14 × (d/2)² × h × 1000

*Example:* d = 2 m, h = 4 m → 3.14 × 1 × 4 × 1000 = **12,560 litres**.

A commonly used guide is about **2.5 g of good bleaching powder per 1000 litres** of water (for routine well disinfection). Dose = 12.56 × 2.5 ≈ **31 g**. Adjust if the powder is weaker (multiply by 33 ÷ actual % available chlorine) or use Horrock's test.

Method: make a thin paste of the powder in a bucket, add water, let lime settle, pour the clear supernatant into the well, mix by lowering and raising the bucket, wait at least 1 hour before use and check residual chlorine.

**Potassium permanganate** was once used for wells but is a weak disinfectant and not recommended for this purpose; chlorination is the method of choice. A 0.1% (1 in 1000) KMnO4 solution = 1 g in 1 litre, sometimes used for washing.

## Result

1. The available chlorine in the given bleaching powder = ___ %.
2. The water sample showed residual chlorine ___ mg/L, pH ___, H2S test ___.
3. Bleaching powder required for the given well = ___ g.

## Precautions

- Store bleaching powder in airtight, dark, cool containers; it loses chlorine in air and light.
- Titrate promptly after adding acid; add starch only near the end point.
- Chlorinate wells preferably at night so the water stands for the contact period.

## Viva questions

1. **What is available chlorine in fresh bleaching powder?** About 33%.
2. **What residual chlorine should remain after 1 hour?** About 0.5 mg/L.
3. **What is Horrock's apparatus used for?** To find the bleaching powder dose for a well.
4. **Why is starch added near the end point?** Starch–iodine gives a sharp blue colour; added early it binds iodine firmly and blurs the end point.
5. **What does a positive H2S strip test indicate?** Probable faecal contamination of water.
practicals.title: Water purification, water testing and bleaching powder dose

# Counselling children on junk foods and balanced diet (simulation)

**Aim:** To counsel school children on the harms of junk food and the importance of a balanced diet, using IEC material and simulated (role-play) counselling.

## Principle

Children copy habits that are easy, tasty and advertised. Junk foods (high in fat, salt and sugar — HFSS) lead to obesity, dental caries and early diabetes and replace healthy food. Counselling works better when it is friendly, uses pictures and games, offers tasty healthy swaps, and involves parents and teachers.

## Requirements

Empty packets of chips, noodles, biscuits and soft drinks (to read labels); a teaspoon and sugar or salt to show the amount in a product; pictures of healthy snacks; a "healthy plate" chart; quiz cards.

## Procedure

1. **Prepare IEC material:** a poster "Swap it!" (chips → roasted chana; cola → lemon water or buttermilk; noodles → vegetable poha or upma; biscuits → fruit or peanuts).
2. **Label-reading demo:** read the nutrition panel of a soft drink; calculate the sugar in teaspoons (grams of sugar ÷ 4 ≈ teaspoons) and show it with real sugar.
3. **Role play:** one student acts as a child who skips breakfast and eats chips daily; another acts as the pharmacist. Use open questions ("What did you eat today?"), listen, praise good habits, give 2–3 simple goals.
4. **Quiz/game:** sort pictures into "everyday foods" and "sometimes foods".
5. Give a take-home sheet for parents.

## Observations

**Sample label calculation:** a 300 ml soft drink with 10.6 g sugar per 100 ml contains about 32 g sugar ≈ **8 teaspoons**.

| Junk food | Main problem | Healthier swap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Potato chips | Salt, fat, no fibre | Roasted chana, makhana, peanuts |
| Soft drinks | Sugar (empty calories) | Water, lemon water, buttermilk, coconut water |
| Instant noodles | Refined flour, salt | Vegetable poha, upma, dalia |
| Fried snacks | Fat, reused oil | Sprouts chaat, fruit |
| Pastries, biscuits | Sugar, trans fat | Fruits, homemade laddu in small amounts |

**Counselling checklist:** greeting and rapport ✓, open questions ✓, listening ✓, simple facts ✓, practical swaps ✓, goal setting ✓, follow-up ✓.

## Result

IEC material was prepared and simulated counselling of children on junk food and balanced diet was carried out.

## Precautions

- Do not shame children about weight or food; be positive.
- Keep facts simple and correct; avoid frightening language.
- Respect food culture and family budget when suggesting swaps.

## Viva questions

1. **What are HFSS foods?** Foods high in fat, salt and sugar.
2. **How many grams of sugar make one teaspoon (approx.)?** About 4 g.
3. **Name two ill effects of junk food in children.** Obesity and dental caries (also early diabetes, poor concentration).
4. **What is IEC?** Information, Education and Communication.
5. **Give two healthy snack swaps.** Roasted chana instead of chips; buttermilk instead of soft drinks.
practicals.title: Counselling children on junk food and balanced diet

# Nutrition charts, local food sources, caloric needs and glycaemic index

**Aim:** To prepare charts on nutrients and their locally available food sources, to calculate the caloric needs of different groups, and to prepare a chart of the glycaemic index of foods.

## Principle

Every nutrient has cheap local sources. Energy needs depend on age, sex, body weight, physical activity and physiological state (pregnancy, lactation). A simple estimate is: **energy need = basal metabolic rate (BMR) × physical activity level (PAL)**. The **glycaemic index (GI)** shows how fast a carbohydrate food raises blood glucose compared with glucose (GI = 100); low-GI foods are better for people with diabetes.

## Requirements

Chart paper, pictures of local foods, food composition tables (ICMR–NIN), weighing scale, calculator.

## Procedure

1. Prepare chart 1: nutrient → function → local sources → deficiency.
2. Prepare chart 2: caloric needs of a child, a pregnant or lactating mother, and a sedentary adult, with the calculation shown.
3. Prepare chart 3: glycaemic index of common foods in three colour bands (low, medium, high).
4. Display and explain the charts.

## Observations

**Chart 1 — local sources (examples for Himachal Pradesh and North India)**

| Nutrient | Local sources |
| --- | --- |
| Energy | Wheat, rice, maize, millets (ragi, bajra), potato, jaggery |
| Protein | Rajma, chana, moong, masoor, soya, milk, curd, paneer, eggs, local fish and meat |
| Iron | Green leaves (spinach, mustard greens, bathua), jaggery, dried fruits, pulses, liver |
| Calcium | Milk, curd, ragi, sesame, green leaves |
| Vitamin A | Carrot, pumpkin, mango, papaya, green leaves, milk, eggs |
| Vitamin C | Amla, guava, citrus fruits, tomato, sprouted pulses |
| Fibre | Whole wheat atta, millets, vegetables, fruits, pulses |

**Chart 2 — caloric needs (approximate method)**

BMR ≈ 1 kcal per kg per hour for men and about 0.9 kcal per kg per hour for women.

| Group | Calculation | Approx. need |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sedentary man, 60 kg | 60 × 24 × 1.0 = 1440 kcal BMR; × PAL 1.5 | ≈ 2160 kcal/day |
| Sedentary woman, 55 kg | 55 × 24 × 0.9 = 1188 kcal BMR; × PAL 1.5 | ≈ 1780 kcal/day |
| Pregnant woman (2nd–3rd trimester) | Her need + about 350 kcal | ≈ 2130 kcal/day (for the woman above) |
| Lactating mother (first 6 months) | Her need + about 600 kcal | ≈ 2380 kcal/day |
| Child, 6 years (rule of thumb) | 1000 + 100 × age in years | ≈ 1600 kcal/day |

PAL values used: sedentary about 1.4–1.5, moderate about 1.7–1.8, heavy work about 2.0 or more. These are estimates for teaching; actual recommended allowances come from ICMR–NIN tables.

**Chart 3 — glycaemic index (approximate)**

| Band | GI | Foods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low | 55 or less | Lentils and dals, rajma, chana, milk, curd, apple, orange, barley |
| Medium | 56–69 | Brown rice, whole wheat roti, banana (ripe), sweet corn |
| High | 70 or more | Glucose, white bread, cornflakes, white rice (some varieties), potato (boiled/mashed), watermelon |

## Result

Charts on nutrients and local sources, caloric needs of different groups, and glycaemic index of foods were prepared and explained.

## Precautions

- Label all values as approximate; quote the source of tables used.
- GI changes with cooking, ripeness and what is eaten together; use it as a guide only.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the glycaemic index?** A measure of how fast a carbohydrate food raises blood glucose compared with glucose (100).
2. **Give two low-GI foods.** Dals/lentils and milk (also apple, rajma).
3. **How much extra energy does a pregnant woman need?** About 350 kcal a day in the second and third trimesters.
4. **Name a cheap local source of vitamin C.** Amla (also guava).
5. **What is PAL?** Physical activity level — the factor by which BMR is multiplied to get total energy need.
practicals.title: Nutrition charts, caloric needs and glycaemic index

# Tobacco cessation counselling and identification of tobacco products

**Aim:** To identify various tobacco-containing products through charts or pictures and to practise tobacco cessation counselling using the 5 As and 5 Rs.

## Principle

Nicotine is highly addictive, and tobacco in any form causes cancers (mouth, throat, lung), heart attack, stroke, COPD and pregnancy problems. Brief advice by a health professional increases quit attempts. The **5 As** guide a willing user; the **5 Rs** motivate an unwilling user. Nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and other medicines double the chance of quitting.

## Requirements

Charts or pictures of tobacco products (no real products need to be handled), NRT samples or pictures (gum, patch, lozenge), a Fagerström dependence questionnaire, role-play cards.

## Procedure

1. Prepare a chart of smoked and smokeless tobacco products used in India.
2. Note the legal points from COTPA 2003 and the ban on e-cigarettes (2019).
3. Role play: pharmacist counsels (a) a willing smoker using the 5 As; (b) an unwilling gutkha user using the 5 Rs.
4. Explain NRT use: gum — "chew and park" between cheek and gum; patch — apply each morning on clean hairless skin, change site daily.
5. Record a quit plan with a quit date.

## Observations

**Tobacco products**

| Smoked | Smokeless |
| --- | --- |
| Cigarettes, bidis, cigars, cheroots, hookah, chillum | Gutkha, khaini, zarda, pan masala with tobacco, mawa, mishri, gul, gudakhu, snuff |
| (E-cigarettes and heat-not-burn devices — banned in India) | Betel quid with tobacco |

**5 As (willing to quit)**

| Step | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Ask | Ask about tobacco use at every visit |
| Advise | Clear, strong, personal advice to quit |
| Assess | Is the person willing to quit now? |
| Assist | Set a quit date, remove tobacco, plan for cravings, offer NRT, refer to cessation centre/quitline |
| Arrange | Follow-up within the first week |

**5 Rs (not yet willing)**: **R**elevance (why quitting matters to them), **R**isks (of continuing), **R**ewards (of quitting — money, health, family), **R**oadblocks (barriers and how to overcome them), **R**epetition (repeat at every visit).

**Benefits after quitting:** better breathing and taste within weeks; heart risk falls over the following year; cancer risk falls over years.

## Result

Tobacco products were identified from charts, and cessation counselling was practised using the 5 As and 5 Rs.

## Precautions

- Be supportive, not judgemental; relapse is common and is part of quitting.
- NRT is used with caution in recent heart attack and pregnancy (doctor's advice).
- Do not handle or sample tobacco products during the practical.

## Viva questions

1. **Which law controls tobacco in India?** COTPA, 2003 (Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act).
2. **What are the 5 As?** Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange.
3. **Name two forms of NRT.** Nicotine gum and nicotine patch (also lozenges).
4. **What is the addictive substance in tobacco?** Nicotine.
5. **Name two smokeless tobacco products.** Gutkha and khaini.

questions.answer:
1. WHO definition (1948): health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. It is a positive and broad idea, though 'complete' well-being is an ideal.
2. Dimensions: (a) Physical – body organs work normally, good appetite, sleep, normal pulse and BP. (b) Mental – able to think clearly, learn and cope with stress. (c) Social – good relations with family and community. (d) Spiritual – values and a sense of purpose. (e) Emotional – feelings expressed and controlled well. (f) Vocational – satisfying work suited to ability. Others: cultural, educational, environmental, nutritional.
3. Determinants: (a) Biological – genes, age, sex (e.g. thalassaemia). (b) Behaviour and lifestyle – smoking, alcohol, diet, exercise. (c) Environment – water, air, housing, vectors, noise, stress. (d) Socio-economic – income, education (especially female literacy), occupation, political system. (e) Health services – availability, cost and quality of care, vaccines and medicines. (f) Others – ageing, gender, mass media, culture.
4. Role of pharmacist: advises on lifestyle, safe water and hygiene, supplies preventive products, screens and refers.
questions.question: Define health as per WHO. Describe the dimensions and determinants of health.

questions.answer:
1. Health is a state subject; the Centre (MoHFW, DGHS) funds national programmes and makes policy; states run services through district, block and village levels.
2. Primary level: Sub-centre (5,000 population; 3,000 in hilly/tribal areas) with ANM and male health worker – immunisation, ANC, family planning; PHC (30,000; 20,000 hilly) with a medical officer, pharmacist and nurses, 4–6 beds; many now upgraded as Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
3. Secondary level: CHC (1,20,000; 80,000 hilly) with specialists and 30 beds, acting as first referral unit; sub-district and district hospitals.
4. Tertiary level: medical colleges, AIIMS and super-speciality hospitals.
5. Other public systems: ESI, CGHS, railway and defence hospitals, AYUSH.
6. Private sector: clinics, nursing homes, corporate hospitals, chemists, labs – large share of outpatient care, costly, variable quality; NGOs and trusts form a voluntary sector.
7. NHM: NRHM (2005) + NUHM (2013). Aim – accessible, affordable, quality care. Components – health system strengthening (free drugs and diagnostics, ambulances), RMNCH+A, communicable and non-communicable disease control. Features – ASHA, JSY, JSSK, RBSK, RKSK, Rogi Kalyan Samitis, village health committees.
8. Pharmacist: manages drug stores, dispenses free medicines and counsels in PHCs and CHCs.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: Social Pharmacy is the branch of pharmacy that studies the social, behavioural, economic and cultural factors affecting medicine use and health, and the pharmacist's role in improving public health.
2. It draws from sociology, psychology, public health, economics, communication and law.
3. Scope: rational use of medicines; health education; disease prevention (immunisation awareness, screening, tobacco cessation); access to affordable generics (Jan Aushadhi); pharmacovigilance; support to national programmes (DOTS, ORS–zinc, IFA, contraceptives); safe disposal of medicines; research on adherence and medicine-use behaviour.
4. Role of pharmacists: most accessible health worker; health educator; counsellor improving adherence; screening (BP, sugar, BMI) and referral (cough > 2 weeks, high-risk pregnancy); supplier of ORS, condoms, sanitary pads, repellents; partner in national programmes; reports ADRs; helps in emergencies; prevents drug misuse.
5. WHO 'seven-star pharmacist': care-giver, decision-maker, communicator, manager, life-long learner, teacher, leader (+ researcher).

Indicators are variables that measure the health status of a community and allow comparison.
Mortality – crude death rate, IMR, MMR, life expectancy.
Morbidity – incidence, prevalence.
Disability – DALY, days of restricted activity.
Nutritional – low birth weight, stunting, wasting, anaemia.
Health-care delivery – doctor–population ratio, beds.
Utilisation – immunisation coverage, institutional deliveries.
Socio-economic – literacy, income, safe water.
Composite – PQLI (IMR, life expectancy at age one, literacy), HDI.

questions.answer:
Goal: highest possible level of health and well-being for all at all ages through preventive and promotive care, and universal access to good quality care without financial hardship.

1. Family planning lets couples decide the number and spacing of children; it improves maternal and child health and controls population growth.
2. Spacing methods: (a) Barrier – male/female condom (also prevents STDs/HIV), diaphragm, spermicides. (b) IUDs – Cu-T 380A (about 10 years), Cu-T 375 (about 5 years), LNG-IUS; copper is toxic to sperm and prevents implantation. (c) Hormonal – combined oral pill (e.g. Mala-N: 21 hormone + 7 iron tablets) stops ovulation; injectable DMPA (Antara) every 3 months; implants; emergency pill (levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 72 h). (d) Non-hormonal pill – centchroman (Chhaya): twice weekly for 3 months, then weekly. (e) Natural – rhythm/calendar, withdrawal, LAM (exclusive breastfeeding, baby < 6 months, no periods).
3. Terminal methods: vasectomy (no-scalpel) and tubectomy (laparoscopic or minilap) – permanent.
4. Pharmacist's role: stock and explain methods; missed-pill rules; ECP is not for regular use; promote condoms for dual protection; privacy and non-judgemental counselling; side effects (spotting, nausea); refer for IUD/sterilisation; support national campaigns.
