questions.answer:
1. Recommendation: start within 1 hour of birth, give colostrum, exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months (no water, honey or ghutti), then complementary foods with breastfeeding up to 2 years or more.
2. Benefits to baby: ideal, easily digested nutrition; antibodies (IgA in colostrum) protect against diarrhoea and pneumonia; less allergy, obesity and diabetes later; better brain development and bonding.
3. Benefits to mother: less bleeding after delivery; natural spacing (LAM); lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer; faster weight loss.
4. Benefits to family/society: free, clean, ready at the right temperature; fewer illnesses and lower costs; environment-friendly.
5. Ill effects of milk substitutes and bottles: infections from unclean bottles and teats (diarrhoea, thrush); over-dilution → malnutrition/marasmus, under-dilution → dehydration and obesity; no antibodies → more infections; cow's milk allergy; costly, needs safe water and fuel; poorer bonding; mother loses natural contraception.
6. IMS Act 1992 (amended 2003) bans promotion of infant milk substitutes and feeding bottles.
7. Pharmacist: counsel and support breastfeeding, do not promote formula, explain safe preparation when formula is medically needed.
questions.question: Explain the importance of breastfeeding. Write the ill effects of infant milk substitutes and bottle feeding.

questions.answer:
1. Immunity: the body's ability to resist infection.
2. Classification: Innate (non-specific: skin, mucus, acid, phagocytes). Acquired – Active (body makes antibodies; slow, long-lasting): natural (after infection), artificial (after vaccine). Passive (ready-made antibodies; quick, short): natural (placenta, breast milk), artificial (immunoglobulins, antitoxins, ASV). Herd immunity protects the unvaccinated when most are immune.
3. Vaccine types: live attenuated (BCG, OPV, MR, rotavirus, varicella); killed/inactivated (IPV, rabies, hepatitis A); toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria); subunit/recombinant (hepatitis B, HPV); conjugate (Hib, PCV, typhoid conjugate); mRNA and vector vaccines.
4. Cold chain: system to keep vaccines at the right temperature from maker to beneficiary. Most vaccines +2 to +8 °C; never freeze Td, pentavalent, hepatitis B, PCV. Equipment – walk-in coolers, ILR, deep freezers, cold boxes, vaccine carriers, ice packs. VVM shows heat exposure (discard if the square is as dark as the circle); shake test detects freezing. OPV is most heat-sensitive; BCG and MR need protection from light.
5. Pharmacist: maintain cold chain, remind about doses, counsel on mild side effects, report AEFI, dispel myths.
questions.question: Define immunity and classify it. Describe the types of vaccines and the cold chain system.

questions.answer:
Household methods: boiling (rolling boil 5–10 minutes; kills all microbes); chemical – bleaching powder, chlorine tablets; filtration – ceramic candle filters; UV and reverse osmosis units; storage in covered vessels with a ladle.
Chlorination: chlorine kills bacteria and viruses; it should leave a free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/L after 1 hour contact. Bleaching powder has about 33% available chlorine and loses strength on storage. Horrock's apparatus finds the dose for wells. Chlorine does not reliably kill amoebic cysts or worm eggs at usual doses.
questions.question: Write the methods of household purification of water. Add a note on chlorination.

questions.answer:
Yellow: anatomical waste, soiled dressings, expired or discarded medicines, chemical waste – incineration or deep burial.
Red: contaminated recyclable plastics – tubing, catheters, IV sets, syringes without needles, gloves – autoclave or microwave, then recycling.
White (translucent, puncture-proof): sharps – needles, blades – autoclave and shredding.
Blue: glassware and metallic implants – disinfection, then recycling.
Segregate at source, never mix with general waste, and label containers.
questions.question: Write the colour coding and treatment of bio-medical waste as per BMW Rules 2016.

questions.answer:
Social impact: poor school and work performance, absenteeism and loss of productivity, poverty, crime and violence, road accidents, domestic violence and family breakdown, HIV and hepatitis by shared needles, stigma, suicide risk.
Health: alcohol – cirrhosis, pancreatitis, Wernicke–Korsakoff; tobacco – oral and lung cancers, heart disease, COPD.
Pharmacist: sell habit-forming drugs only on valid prescription and keep records; watch repeated purchases; educate youth; brief cessation advice (5 As), nicotine replacement; refer to de-addiction centres; follow NDPS Act 1985 and COTPA 2003.
questions.question: Discuss the social impact of alcohol and tobacco use and the role of the pharmacist in preventing substance abuse.

questions.answer:
Diseases caused by the work environment. Dust: pneumoconioses – silicosis, asbestosis, anthracosis (coal), byssinosis (cotton), bagassosis (sugarcane), farmer's lung. Chemicals: lead and mercury poisoning, benzene, dermatitis. Physical: noise-induced deafness, heat, radiation. Biological: anthrax, brucellosis, hepatitis B (health workers). Ergonomic: back pain, accidents. Psychosocial: stress.
Prevention: engineering control (ventilation, wet methods, enclosure), personal protective equipment, pre-placement and periodic examination, health education; Factories Act 1948, ESI Act 1948.
questions.question: Write a note on occupational illnesses and their prevention.

questions.answer:
Sources: factory effluents, hospital waste, excretion of drugs by people and animals, flushing or throwing unused medicines.
Effects: antibiotic residues promote antimicrobial resistance; hormones (ethinyl-oestradiol) feminise fish; veterinary diclofenac caused vulture decline in India (now banned for veterinary use); contamination of water and soil.
Prevention: effluent treatment plants, green chemistry, take-back of unused medicines, BMW segregation, never flush medicines, dispense only needed quantities, public education by pharmacists.
questions.question: How do pharmaceuticals cause environmental pollution? How can it be prevented?

questions.answer:
Demography = study of population size, composition, distribution and change.
Stage 1 – high stationary: high birth and death rates, slow growth.
Stage 2 – early expanding: death rate falls, birth rate stays high, rapid growth.
Stage 3 – late expanding: birth rate also starts to fall (India is here).
Stage 4 – low stationary: low birth and death rates, stable population.
Stage 5 – declining: birth rate below death rate.
Indicators: birth rate, death rate, growth rate, TFR (2.1 = replacement), sex ratio, dependency ratio.
questions.question: Explain the demographic cycle.

questions.answer: BCG, oral polio vaccine (OPV), measles–rubella (MR) vaccine and rotavirus vaccine (also varicella, yellow fever).
questions.question: Name any four live attenuated vaccines.

questions.answer: A heat-sensitive label (square inside a circle) on a vaccine vial. If the square becomes as dark as or darker than the circle, the vaccine has been exposed to too much heat and must be discarded.
questions.question: What is a vaccine vial monitor?

questions.answer: Misuse: using a medicine for a purpose or in a way not intended (e.g. extra sleeping pills). Abuse: self-administration, usually for pleasure, in a way that harms health or social functioning.
questions.question: Differentiate drug misuse and drug abuse.

questions.answer:
1. Balanced diet: a diet containing all nutrients in the right amounts and proportions to meet the body's needs, keep a small reserve and maintain health. About 50–60% energy from carbohydrates, 10–15% from proteins, 20–30% from fats.
2. Macronutrients: Carbohydrates (4 kcal/g) – main energy source; cereals, millets, tubers, sugar. Proteins (4 kcal/g) – body-building, enzymes, antibodies; pulses, milk, egg, meat; cereal + pulse gives complete protein; deficiency → PEM (kwashiorkor, marasmus). Fats (9 kcal/g) – concentrated energy, fat-soluble vitamins, essential fatty acids; oils, ghee, nuts.
3. Micronutrients – vitamins: A (night blindness, xerophthalmia), D (rickets, osteomalacia), K (bleeding), B1 (beriberi), B2 (angular stomatitis), B3 (pellagra), folate and B12 (megaloblastic anaemia), C (scurvy).
4. Minerals: iron (anaemia), iodine (goitre, cretinism), calcium (rickets, osteoporosis), zinc (growth failure), fluoride (caries if low, fluorosis if high).
5. Water and fibre also needed.
6. Food groups: cereals, pulses, milk and animal foods, vegetables and fruits, fats and sugar.
7. Pharmacist: diet counselling, supplements when needed, avoid overdose of vitamins A and D and iron.
questions.question: Define balanced diet. Describe the macronutrients and micronutrients with their sources and deficiency diseases.

questions.answer:
1. Adulteration: adding cheaper or harmful substances, removing valuable parts, or selling spoiled food as good. Controlled by the FSS Act 2006 through FSSAI.
2. Examples: milk – water, starch, urea, detergent; ghee – vanaspati; mustard oil – argemone oil (epidemic dropsy); arhar dal – khesari dal (lathyrism); turmeric – metanil yellow, lead chromate; chilli powder – brick powder, colours; black pepper – papaya seeds; tea – used leaves, colour; coffee – chicory; sweets – non-permitted colours.
3. Simple tests: iodine turns starch-adulterated milk blue; papaya seeds float in spirit; brick powder settles fast in water.
4. Artificial ripening: calcium carbide gives acetylene and carries arsenic and phosphorus traces; causes headache, dizziness, vomiting, mouth and stomach ulcers, skin and eye irritation; banned; ethylene in controlled chambers is permitted. Signs: patchy colour, bland taste.
5. Pesticides: residues cause acute poisoning (organophosphates) and long-term nerve, hormone and possible cancer effects; controlled by MRLs, bans and integrated pest management; wash and peel produce.
6. Pharmacist: educate consumers, encourage buying FSSAI-licensed products, report suspected adulteration.
questions.question: What is food adulteration? List common adulterants with their health effects. Add notes on artificial ripening of fruits and pesticide residues.

questions.answer:
1. Dietary supplement: product taken by mouth to add nutrients to the diet (vitamins, minerals, proteins, herbs).
2. Nutraceutical: food or part of food giving medical or health benefits, including prevention of disease (nutrition + pharmaceutical); regulated by FSSAI in India.
3. Examples: IFA and calcium + vitamin D (pregnancy, osteoporosis); multivitamins (poor diet, elderly); omega-3 (high triglycerides); probiotics (antibiotic-associated diarrhoea); prebiotics; protein powders (undernutrition, recovery); glucosamine (osteoarthritis); psyllium (constipation, cholesterol).
4. Cautions: not a substitute for diet; toxicity of vitamins A, D and iron; quality and claims vary; interactions.
5. Drug–food interactions: milk/antacids + tetracycline or ciprofloxacin → chelation, less absorption; grapefruit juice + felodipine/simvastatin → raised levels (CYP3A4); tyramine foods + MAOIs → hypertensive crisis; vitamin K-rich greens + warfarin → less effect; alcohol + metronidazole → disulfiram-like reaction; high protein + levodopa → less effect; fatty meal + griseofulvin → better absorption; rifampicin, levothyroxine, alendronate on empty stomach.
6. Pharmacist: clear timing instructions relative to food, alcohol warnings, review supplements.
questions.question: Define nutraceuticals and dietary supplements with examples and indications. Explain drug–food interactions with examples.

questions.answer:
Kwashiorkor: mainly protein deficiency; age 1–3 years after weaning; oedema present; puffy moon face; flaky-paint skin; sparse, pale or reddish hair ('red boy'); fatty enlarged liver; poor appetite, apathy.
Marasmus: energy and protein deficiency; usually under 1 year; no oedema; severe wasting, 'old man' face, skin and bones; liver normal; good appetite.
Both are forms of protein–energy malnutrition; treat with gradual feeding, treatment of infections and micronutrients.
questions.question: Differentiate kwashiorkor and marasmus.

questions.answer:
Junk (HFSS) food is high in calories, fat, salt or sugar and low in protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre – chips, instant noodles, fried snacks, soft drinks, burgers, pastries.
Ill effects: obesity in children and adults; type 2 diabetes, high BP, high cholesterol, early heart disease; dental caries; acidity and constipation; tiredness and poor concentration; micronutrient deficiencies because it replaces healthy food; harmful additives and reused oils.
Advice: home-cooked food, fruits, read labels, limit sugary drinks.
questions.question: Write the ill effects of junk food.

questions.answer:
Fortification: adding vitamins or minerals to commonly eaten foods to prevent deficiencies in the whole population without changing food habits.
Examples: iodised salt (IDD); double-fortified salt with iodine and iron; rice and wheat flour with iron, folic acid and B12 (anaemia); edible oil and milk with vitamins A and D. FSSAI marks fortified foods with the '+F' logo.
Related: enrichment (restoring nutrients lost in processing) and biofortification (breeding nutrient-rich crops such as iron-rich pearl millet).
questions.question: What is food fortification? Give examples used in India.

questions.answer:
Water: about 60% of body weight; solvent and transport medium, temperature control, digestion, excretion of wastes, lubrication; adult needs roughly 2–3 L/day, more in heat, fever, diarrhoea; dehydration causes dizziness, low urine, stones, constipation.
Fibre: indigestible plant part. Soluble (oats, pulses, isabgol) lowers cholesterol and sugar rise; insoluble (bran, whole grains, vegetables) adds bulk and prevents constipation, piles and diverticulosis; gives fullness (weight control); feeds gut bacteria; low fibre linked with colon cancer.
questions.question: Write the importance of water and dietary fibre in the diet.

questions.answer:
GM foods come from organisms whose DNA has been changed by genetic engineering to add a trait.
Benefits: pest resistance (Bt crops) and less pesticide, higher yield, drought or salt tolerance, better nutrition (golden rice with beta-carotene), longer shelf life.
Concerns: allergy to new proteins, gene flow to wild plants, loss of biodiversity, pest resistance, dependence on seed companies, labelling and ethical issues.
In India, approval is by the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC); Bt cotton is the main commercial GM crop.
questions.question: Write a note on genetically modified foods.

questions.answer:
Calorific value is the energy a food gives, usually in kcal per 100 g; nutritive value is its content of protein, fat, vitamins and minerals.
Energy = 4 × carbohydrate (g) + 4 × protein (g) + 9 × fat (g).
Example: 20 g carbohydrate, 2 g protein, 10 g fat = 80 + 8 + 90 = 178 kcal.
Approximate values per 100 g: rice ~345, wheat flour ~340, groundnut ~560, sugar ~400 (empty calories), oil ~900, cow's milk ~65–70 kcal.
questions.question: Explain the calorific value of foods and how to calculate energy from a food label.

questions.answer: Vitamin A: night blindness, Bitot's spots, xerophthalmia, keratomalacia. Vitamin C: scurvy (bleeding gums, poor wound healing).
questions.question: Name the deficiency diseases of vitamin A and vitamin C.

questions.answer: Argemone oil mixed in mustard oil causes epidemic dropsy (oedema, heart failure, glaucoma).
questions.question: Which adulterant causes epidemic dropsy?

questions.answer: Tetracycline with milk – chelation reduces absorption. MAO inhibitors with tyramine-rich cheese – hypertensive crisis.
questions.question: Give two examples of drug–food interactions.

questions.answer:
1. Epidemiology: study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states in populations and the use of this study to control health problems.
2. Applications: finding causes and risk factors; measuring disease burden (incidence, prevalence); natural history of disease; planning and evaluating services and programmes; investigating and controlling outbreaks; testing vaccines and drugs; identifying high-risk groups.
3. Epidemiological triad: agent, host, environment; chain of infection – reservoir, exit, transmission, entry, susceptible host.
4. Terms: Endemic – constant usual presence in an area (malaria in some districts). Epidemic – cases clearly more than expected (cholera after floods). Pandemic – epidemic across countries/continents (COVID-19). Outbreak – small localised epidemic (food poisoning after a feast). Incubation period – time from entry of agent to first symptoms. Isolation – separating sick persons. Quarantine – restricting healthy contacts for the longest incubation period. Contact tracing – finding, testing and monitoring people exposed to a case. Morbidity – illness; mortality – death in a population.
5. Modes of transmission: direct (contact, droplet, soil, transplacental) and indirect (vehicle, vector, airborne, fomites, hands).
questions.question: Define epidemiology and give its applications. Explain the terms epidemic, endemic, pandemic, outbreak, incubation period, isolation, quarantine and contact tracing.

questions.answer:
1. Agent: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus.
2. Transmission: droplet nuclei from coughing patients with lung TB; risk higher with HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, smoking, overcrowding.
3. Clinical features: cough for 2 weeks or more, evening fever, night sweats, weight and appetite loss, haemoptysis, chest pain; extra-pulmonary TB in lymph nodes, spine, brain, abdomen.
4. Diagnosis: sputum microscopy, CBNAAT/Truenat, chest X-ray.
5. Treatment (NTEP, drug-sensitive): 2 months HRZE then 4 months HRE as daily fixed-dose combinations; drug-resistant TB needs special regimens.
6. Prevention: BCG at birth; early detection and complete treatment; preventive therapy for contacts and HIV patients; cough etiquette, masks, ventilation; nutrition support (Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana).
7. Pharmacist: refer presumptive TB; treatment supporter; ensure adherence; counsel on orange urine (rifampicin), jaundice, vision problems (ethambutol), pyridoxine with isoniazid; notify cases; keep records of anti-TB drug sales.
questions.question: Describe the causative agent, mode of transmission, clinical features, treatment and prevention of tuberculosis. Add the role of the pharmacist.

questions.answer:
1. Malaria: agent Plasmodium vivax (commonest), P. falciparum (most dangerous), P. malariae, P. ovale; vector female Anopheles (night biter, clean water). Features: fever with chills and rigors then sweating, headache, anaemia, splenomegaly; falciparum may cause cerebral malaria and kidney failure; vivax relapses. Diagnosis: RDT, blood smear. Treatment: vivax – chloroquine 3 days + primaquine 14 days; falciparum – ACT + single-dose primaquine; severe – injectable artesunate.
2. Dengue: dengue virus 1–4; vector Aedes aegypti (day biter, breeds in clean water in coolers, tyres, pots); incubation 4–7 days. Features: sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind eyes, muscle and joint pain, rash, low platelets; warning signs – abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding → DHF/DSS. Treatment: fluids, paracetamol; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs. Diagnosis: NS1, IgM.
3. Prevention: remove breeding sites (weekly dry day), insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, larvivorous fish, larvicides, repellents, full-sleeve clothes, window screens.
4. Pharmacist: insist on testing before antimalarials; complete course; paracetamol not NSAIDs in fever; promote nets and repellents; refer warning signs; support NVBDCP campaigns.
questions.question: Describe the epidemiology, clinical features and prevention of malaria and dengue. What is the role of the pharmacist?

questions.answer:
1. Influenza: influenza virus A, B, C (orthomyxovirus); droplets; incubation 1–3 days; sudden fever, chills, headache, body ache, sore throat, cough. Antigenic drift → yearly epidemics; antigenic shift → pandemics. Avian flu (H5N1) passes from poultry to humans; H1N1 caused the 2009 pandemic. Treatment: rest, fluids, paracetamol, oseltamivir for high-risk cases.
2. COVID-19: SARS-CoV-2; droplets, aerosols, surfaces; incubation 2–14 days (often ~5); fever, dry cough, sore throat, tiredness, loss of smell and taste, breathlessness; severe in elderly and those with diabetes or heart disease; RT-PCR and rapid antigen tests; WHO declared a pandemic in March 2020.
3. SARS (SARS-CoV, 2002–03) and MERS (MERS-CoV, 2012, camels) – coronavirus diseases with severe pneumonia.
4. Prevention: vaccination (yearly flu vaccine for elderly, pregnant women, health workers; COVID-19 vaccines), masks, cough and sneeze etiquette, hand hygiene, ventilation, distancing, isolation of cases, quarantine of contacts, contact tracing.
5. Pharmacist: educate on etiquette and masks, supply sanitisers and masks, avoid antibiotics for viral illness, identify high-risk patients for referral, counter misinformation.
questions.question: Describe the respiratory infections influenza and COVID-19 with their prevention. Add notes on SARS and MERS.

questions.answer:
Cholera: Vibrio cholerae O1/O139; incubation hours to 5 days; profuse painless rice-water stools, vomiting, severe dehydration. Treatment: ORS, IV Ringer lactate if severe, doxycycline.
Acute diarrhoea: 3 or more loose stools in 24 h; rotavirus, E. coli, Shigella. Assess dehydration (sunken eyes, thirst, slow skin pinch).
Management: low-osmolarity ORS (245 mOsm/L), zinc for 14 days (10 mg < 6 months, 20 mg > 6 months), continue feeding, antibiotics only for dysentery or cholera, no anti-motility drugs in children.
Prevention: safe water, sanitation, hand-washing, breastfeeding, rotavirus vaccine.
questions.question: Write a note on cholera and acute diarrhoeal diseases with management.

questions.answer:
Agent: human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1, HIV-2), a retrovirus destroying CD4 T-cells.
Transmission: unprotected sex, infected blood and shared needles, mother to child (pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding). Not by touch, hugs, food or mosquitoes.
Course: acute flu-like illness → long symptom-free period → AIDS with opportunistic infections (TB commonest).
Treatment: lifelong ART (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir first-line).
Prevention: condoms, screened blood, sterile needles, PPTCT, post-exposure prophylaxis, ICTC testing, awareness (NACP).
questions.question: Write the causative agent, transmission and prevention of HIV/AIDS.

questions.answer:
Agent: Salmonella Typhi; spread by food and water contaminated by patients or carriers (gall bladder).
Incubation: usually 10–14 days.
Features: step-ladder fever, headache, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhoea, coated tongue, relative bradycardia, rose spots, splenomegaly; complications – intestinal bleeding and perforation.
Diagnosis: blood culture early, Widal later.
Treatment: antibiotics per sensitivity (azithromycin, ceftriaxone), full course.
Prevention: safe water and food, sanitation, treating carriers, typhoid vaccines (Vi polysaccharide, conjugate, Ty21a).
questions.question: Describe typhoid fever.

questions.answer:
Measles: measles virus; airborne/droplet; incubation ~10 days to fever; fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik's spots, then rash from face downwards; complications pneumonia, diarrhoea, encephalitis, malnutrition; give vitamin A; prevent with MR vaccine at 9–12 and 16–24 months.
Rubella: rubella virus; incubation 2–3 weeks; mild fever, pink rash, swollen posterior neck and ear glands; in early pregnancy causes congenital rubella syndrome (cataract, deafness, heart defects); prevented by MR vaccine.
questions.question: Write about measles and rubella.

questions.answer:
Agent: Mycobacterium leprae; spread by prolonged close contact (nasal droplets of untreated patients); long incubation of several years.
Features: pale or reddish anaesthetic skin patches, thickened tender nerves, weakness and deformities of hands and feet.
Types: PB (up to 5 patches) and MB (more than 5, or nerve involvement, or smear positive).
Treatment: MDT – rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine; 6 months PB, 12 months MB (WHO recommends three drugs for both); free under NLEP.
Prevention: early detection, contact examination, single-dose rifampicin for contacts, disability care, reducing stigma.
questions.question: Write a note on leprosy.

questions.answer:
Diphtheria: Corynebacterium diphtheriae; droplets; incubation 2–6 days; sore throat, fever, greyish membrane on tonsils, bull neck, airway block; toxin causes myocarditis and nerve palsy; treat with antitoxin + penicillin/erythromycin.
Whooping cough: Bordetella pertussis; incubation 7–14 days; catarrhal, paroxysmal (cough bouts ending in a whoop, vomiting) and convalescent stages; dangerous in infants; treat with azithromycin/erythromycin.
Prevention of both: pentavalent and DPT boosters, Td.
questions.question: Describe diphtheria and whooping cough.

questions.answer:
Agent: poliovirus types 1, 2, 3 (enterovirus); faeco-oral spread; incubation usually 7–14 days.
Most infections are silent; some cause acute flaccid paralysis – sudden, asymmetric floppy weakness, usually of legs, without sensory loss.
Prevention: OPV and IPV in UIP; Pulse Polio campaigns; surveillance of all acute flaccid paralysis in children under 15; sanitation and safe water.
India was certified polio-free in 2014; vaccination continues as the virus exists elsewhere.
questions.question: Write a note on poliomyelitis.

questions.answer:
Tetanus: Clostridium tetani spores from soil enter wounds or the umbilical cord; incubation usually 6–10 days; lockjaw, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, painful spasms; neonatal tetanus from unclean cord cutting. Treatment: tetanus immunoglobulin, wound care, metronidazole, muscle relaxants. Prevention: pentavalent/DPT, Td for pregnant women, clean delivery, Td booster for dirty wounds.
Trachoma: Chlamydia trachomatis; spread by eye discharge via hands, towels, flies; follicles → lid scarring → trichiasis → blindness. Control by SAFE: Surgery, Antibiotics (azithromycin), Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement.
questions.question: Write about tetanus and trachoma.

questions.answer:
Illness from food contaminated with microbes or toxins; many people eating the same meal fall ill.
Staphylococcus aureus (milk sweets; 1–6 h; vomiting), Bacillus cereus (reheated fried rice; vomiting), Salmonella (eggs, poultry; 12–24 h or more; fever, diarrhoea), Clostridium perfringens (meat dishes kept warm; 8–24 h), Clostridium botulinum (badly canned foods; 12–36 h; descending paralysis – needs antitoxin).
Prevention: cook thoroughly, eat hot or refrigerate quickly, hygiene of food handlers, discard swollen cans.
Treatment: ORS and supportive care; botulism is an emergency.
questions.question: Write a note on food poisoning.

questions.answer:
Syphilis (Treponema pallidum) – painless chancre, later rash and heart/brain damage; gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) – urethral pus; chlamydia – often silent, infertility; chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) – painful ulcer; genital herpes (HSV-2) – recurrent painful blisters; trichomoniasis – frothy discharge; genital warts (HPV).
Syndromic management: treat the syndrome (urethral discharge, genital ulcer, vaginal discharge) at first visit with standard kits, treat partners, counsel on condoms, test for HIV and syphilis.
Pharmacist: confidential counselling, condom supply, discourage self-treatment, refer to STI clinics.
questions.question: Write about common sexually transmitted diseases and their syndromic management.

questions.answer: Isolation separates infected (sick) persons to prevent spread. Quarantine restricts movement of healthy contacts for the longest incubation period of the disease.
questions.question: Differentiate isolation and quarantine.

questions.answer: The time between the entry of an infectious agent into the body and the appearance of the first signs or symptoms of disease.
questions.question: What is incubation period?

questions.answer: Malaria – female Anopheles; dengue – Aedes aegypti; filariasis – Culex quinquefasciatus (W. bancrofti) and Mansonia (B. malayi).
questions.question: Name the vectors of malaria, dengue and filariasis.

questions.answer:
1. Background: earlier RNTCP; renamed NTEP in 2020 with the aim of ending TB in line with SDGs.
2. Objectives: reduce TB cases and deaths, ensure free quality diagnosis and treatment, and protect families from catastrophic costs.
3. Strategy – Detect: active case finding in high-risk groups; rapid molecular tests (CBNAAT, Truenat); notification by private sector.
4. Treat: free daily fixed-dose combinations (2HRZE + 4HRE for drug-sensitive TB); regimens for drug-resistant TB; treatment supporters; adherence monitoring.
5. Prevent: BCG; TB preventive therapy for contacts and people with HIV; airborne infection control.
6. Build: Ni-kshay online system; Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (nutrition support by direct benefit transfer); Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan with community Ni-kshay Mitras; inter-sectoral partnerships.
7. Outcome: wider free access to rapid tests and drugs; better notification from private sector.
8. Pharmacist: refer cough ≥ 2 weeks; act as treatment supporter; counsel on side effects and adherence; notify cases; maintain records of anti-TB drug sales; avoid irregular private treatment.
questions.question: Describe the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme with its objectives, components and the role of pharmacists.

questions.answer:
1. NVBDCP covers six diseases: malaria, dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic filariasis, Japanese encephalitis and kala-azar; now under the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control.
2. NVBDCP objectives: prevent and control vector-borne diseases; eliminate malaria, filariasis and kala-azar.
3. NVBDCP components: early diagnosis (RDT, microscopy) and complete treatment; integrated vector management – long-lasting insecticidal nets, indoor residual spraying, larvivorous fish, source reduction, larvicides; mass drug administration for filariasis with morbidity care; JE vaccination in endemic areas; surveillance and behaviour change communication.
4. NACP (run by NACO and State AIDS Control Societies) objectives: prevent new HIV infections and give care, support and treatment, reducing stigma.
5. NACP components: targeted interventions for high-risk groups; condom promotion; needle-syringe exchange and opioid substitution; ICTC testing; PPTCT; free ART centres; blood safety; STI clinics with syndromic management; IEC; HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act 2017.
6. Pharmacist: rational antimalarial use and paracetamol in dengue; promote nets and repellents; supply condoms discreetly; ART adherence counselling; confidentiality; refer for testing.
questions.question: Write about the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme and the National AIDS Control Programme.

questions.answer:
1. General role: drug logistics and cold chain; dispensing and counselling for adherence; health education and health days; screening and referral; reporting cases, ADRs and AEFI; promoting rational use and generics (Jan Aushadhi); working with ASHA, ANM and NGOs; help in disasters and mass drug administration.
2. NP-NCD (earlier NPCDCS): prevents and controls cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and stroke. Components: population-based screening of adults 30 years and above for BP, diabetes and oral, breast and cervical cancer at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs; NCD clinics at CHC and district hospital; free drugs; lifestyle counselling; cardiac and cancer care.
3. NMHP: aims at minimum mental health care for all, integration with general health care and community participation. Components: District Mental Health Programme, training of doctors and workers, suicide prevention, school mental health, Tele-MANAS helpline 14416; Mental Healthcare Act 2017.
4. Pharmacist in these: BP and sugar checks, adherence counselling, insulin technique, recognise depression and suicide risk, safe storage of sedatives.
questions.question: Explain the role of pharmacists in national health programmes. Give brief notes on NP-NCD and the National Mental Health Programme.

questions.answer:
UIP gives free vaccines to children and pregnant women: BCG, OPV, IPV, hepatitis B, pentavalent, rotavirus, PCV, MR, JE (endemic districts), DPT boosters, Td.
Support: cold chain, eVIN stock monitoring, AEFI surveillance, sessions at sub-centres and outreach.
Mission Indradhanush and its intensified rounds are catch-up drives to vaccinate children and women who missed doses.
Outcomes: polio-free certification (2014); maternal and neonatal tetanus eliminated (2015).
Pharmacist: cold chain, reminders, AEFI reporting, dispelling myths.
questions.question: Write a note on the Universal Immunization Programme and Mission Indradhanush.

questions.answer:
Ayushman Bharat (2018): (1) Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (earlier Health and Wellness Centres) – upgraded sub-centres and PHCs providing comprehensive primary care including NCD screening, mental health, elderly care, free medicines and tests; (2) PM-JAY – health insurance for hospital care of poor and vulnerable families in empanelled public and private hospitals.
PMBJP: Jan Aushadhi Kendras sell quality generic medicines at low prices, run by pharmacists; also sell low-cost sanitary napkins. Reduces out-of-pocket spending.
questions.question: Write a note on Ayushman Bharat and Jan Aushadhi.

questions.answer:
Objective: reduce leprosy burden, prevent disability and interrupt transmission.
Components: early case detection by active search and awareness campaigns; free MDT blister packs; single-dose rifampicin post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts; disability prevention and medical rehabilitation (self-care, footwear, reconstructive surgery); reducing stigma.
Outcome: elimination as a public health problem at national level (prevalence below 1 per 10,000) in 2005; new cases still found.
Pharmacist: refer anaesthetic patches, counsel on MDT (clofazimine skin colour, red urine), adherence.
questions.question: Write a note on the National Leprosy Eradication Programme.

questions.answer:
Objectives: awareness of harms of tobacco, help users quit, enforce tobacco laws.

1. Definition: branch of health economics that identifies, measures and compares the costs and consequences of drug therapy and pharmaceutical services.
2. Costs: direct medical (drugs, fees, tests, hospital stay); direct non-medical (travel, food and stay for attendants, special diet); indirect (lost productivity, wages, early death); intangible (pain, anxiety, suffering). Also fixed, variable, opportunity and incremental costs.
3. Outcomes: ECHO – economic, clinical, humanistic.
4. Cost-minimisation analysis: outcomes proven equal; choose the cheaper (brand vs bioequivalent generic).
5. Cost-effectiveness analysis: outcomes in clinical units (mmHg, cures, life-years); cost per unit outcome; ICER = difference in cost ÷ difference in effect.
6. Cost-benefit analysis: costs and outcomes in money; benefit-to-cost ratio > 1 or net benefit > 0 is worthwhile; valuing life in money is a drawback.
7. Cost-utility analysis: outcomes in QALYs (years × utility 0–1); cost per QALY gained.
8. Perspective (patient, provider, payer, society) and sensitivity analysis must be stated.

questions.answer:
1. Importance: limited health budgets and high out-of-pocket spending in India; helps choose best value.
2. Uses: hospital formulary decisions; NLEM selection; drug price control by NPPA under DPCO; deciding coverage in PM-JAY and insurance; Health Technology Assessment in India (HTAIn); standard treatment guidelines; generic prescribing; drug development value claims; lower costs for patients and better adherence.
3. Steps: define the problem; choose perspective; identify alternatives; choose method (CMA, CEA, CBA, CUA); identify and measure costs and outcomes; discount future values; analyse (ratios, ICER, decision tree); sensitivity analysis; present results and decide.
4. Pharmacist: suggests generic substitutes and Jan Aushadhi products; avoids irrational drugs; improves adherence; reduces inventory wastage and expiry; collects cost and outcome data; counsels on the cheapest effective option.

questions.answer:
CEA: outcome in natural clinical units (mmHg reduced, patients cured, life-years gained); result as cost per unit of effect or ICER; used for options with the same kind of outcome. Example: drug A ₹200 controls 60/100 patients, drug B ₹500 controls 75/100; ICER = ₹30,000 ÷ 15 = ₹2,000 per extra patient controlled.
CBA: costs and outcomes both in money; result as benefit-to-cost ratio or net benefit; can compare programmes with different outcomes. Example: vaccination drive costing ₹10 lakh saves ₹40 lakh → ratio 4:1.

questions.answer:
Direct medical: medicines, doctor fees, laboratory tests, hospital stay, surgery, nursing.
Direct non-medical: travel, food and lodging of attendants, special diets, child care.
Indirect: productivity lost due to illness or early death – lost wages, school days.
Intangible: pain, anxiety, grief, stigma – hard to put in money.
Other terms: fixed cost (rent, equipment), variable cost (drugs, syringes), opportunity cost (best alternative given up), incremental cost (extra cost of one option over another), average cost.

questions.answer:
QALY (quality-adjusted life year) = years of life × utility (0 = death, 1 = perfect health). 4 years at 0.5 = 2 QALYs; used in cost-utility analysis as cost per QALY gained.
DALY (disability-adjusted life year) = years of life lost due to early death + years lived with disability weighted for severity; measures disease burden. Example: 10 years lost + 5 years at disability weight 0.4 = 12 DALYs. One DALY = one lost year of healthy life.

It is the simplest analysis; its main limitation is that equal outcomes must truly be proven, otherwise CEA is needed.
Example: generic amlodipine ₹15 vs brand ₹60 per strip with equal effect → generic preferred.

# Unit 1: Introduction to Social Pharmacy

Social Pharmacy looks at medicines and pharmacists from the side of **society**: how people get, use and misuse medicines, what keeps a community healthy, and how a pharmacist can help the public stay well, not only dispense tablets.

## 1.1 Definition and scope of Social Pharmacy

**Definition.** Social Pharmacy is the branch of pharmacy that studies the social, behavioural, economic and cultural factors that affect the use of medicines and the health of people, and the role of the pharmacist in improving public health.

In simple words: pharmaceutics asks *"how is the tablet made?"*; social pharmacy asks *"will the patient actually get it, take it correctly, afford it, and stay healthy?"*

**Social Pharmacy as a discipline** borrows ideas from several subjects:

| Subject it borrows from | What it adds |
| --- | --- |
| Sociology and psychology | Beliefs, habits, self-medication, compliance |
| Public health and epidemiology | Disease patterns, prevention, health programmes |
| Economics | Cost of medicines, affordability, pharmacoeconomics |
| Communication sciences | Counselling, health education, IEC materials |
| Law and ethics | Drug laws, rational use, patient rights |

**Scope of Social Pharmacy in improving public health**

1. **Rational use of medicines** — right drug, right dose, right duration, right price; fighting irrational fixed-dose combinations and antibiotic misuse.
2. **Health education** — teaching the public about hygiene, nutrition, vaccines, family planning and danger signs of diseases.
3. **Disease prevention** — immunisation awareness, screening camps (blood pressure, blood sugar), tobacco and alcohol cessation.
4. **Access to medicines** — generic medicines, Jan Aushadhi stores, free-drug schemes of government hospitals.
5. **Pharmacovigilance** — reporting adverse drug reactions and medicine quality problems.
6. **Support to national health programmes** — DOTS for TB, ORS and zinc for diarrhoea, iron–folic acid, condoms and oral pills.
7. **Safe disposal of medicines** and reducing environmental pollution from pharmaceuticals.
8. **Research** on medicine-use behaviour, adherence and community needs.

## 1.2 Role of pharmacists in public health

The community pharmacist is often the **most accessible health professional** — no appointment, no fee, open long hours, present even in small towns. This makes the pharmacy a natural "first point of contact".

**Key public-health roles**

- **Health promoter and educator:** advice on diet, exercise, hygiene, safe water, breastfeeding.
- **Counsellor:** explains dose, timing, side effects, storage; improves adherence in TB, HIV, diabetes, hypertension.
- **Screener and referrer:** checks BP, blood glucose, BMI; refers suspected TB (cough > 2 weeks), malaria, high-risk pregnancy to a doctor or PHC.
- **Supplier of preventive products:** ORS, zinc, condoms, sanitary pads, mosquito repellents, iodised salt advice.
- **Partner in national programmes:** DOTS provider, family planning distributor, vaccination awareness.
- **Pharmacovigilance and drug information:** reports adverse reactions, answers drug queries.
- **Responding in emergencies and disasters:** first aid, emergency supply of medicines.
- **Fighting misuse:** refuses to sell habit-forming drugs without prescription, counsels on tobacco and alcohol.

**The "seven-star pharmacist" (WHO idea, extended by FIP)**

```text
          Care-giver
   Leader             Decision-maker
 Manager      PHARMACIST      Communicator
   Teacher            Life-long learner
       (+ Researcher = "eight-star" pharmacist)
```

## 1.3 Concept of health

### WHO definition (1948)

> Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

Points to note:

- It is **positive** — health is not just "no disease".
- It is **broad** — body, mind and social life all count.
- Criticism: "complete" well-being is an ideal that few people ever reach; it is hard to measure. Later, the idea of a socially and economically productive life was added to health goals ("Health for All").

### Dimensions of health

| Dimension | Meaning | Example of good health |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physical | Body works normally | Normal pulse, BP, weight; good sleep and appetite |
| Mental | Ability to think, learn, handle stress | Free from anxiety disorders; good self-esteem |
| Social | Getting on well with others | Good family and community relations |
| Spiritual | Sense of purpose, values | Inner peace, meaning in life |
| Emotional | Feelings handled well | Can express and control emotions |
| Vocational | Satisfaction from work | Job matches ability; work brings achievement |

Other dimensions sometimes listed: philosophical, cultural, educational, environmental, nutritional and preventive.

### Determinants of health (what decides how healthy a person is)

```text
              Biological (genes, age, sex)
                        |
 Behaviour/lifestyle --- HEALTH --- Environment (water, air, housing)
                        |
   Socio-economic (income, education, job) + Health services
```

1. **Biological/genetic** — inherited diseases (thalassaemia, haemophilia), sex, age.
2. **Behavioural and lifestyle** — smoking, alcohol, diet, exercise, sexual behaviour.
3. **Environmental** — physical (water, air, noise, housing), biological (vectors, microbes), psychosocial (stress, family).
4. **Socio-economic** — income, education (especially female literacy), occupation, political system.
5. **Health services** — availability, cost and quality of hospitals, medicines and vaccines.
6. **Ageing, gender, and others** — e.g. industrial growth, mass media, cultural beliefs.

### Health indicators

An **indicator** is a variable that helps measure the health of a community and to compare places or years.

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Mortality | Crude death rate, infant mortality rate (IMR), under-5 mortality, maternal mortality ratio (MMR), life expectancy |
| Morbidity | Incidence and prevalence of diseases, hospital admissions |
| Disability | Days of restricted activity, DALY (disability-adjusted life years) |
| Nutritional status | Low birth weight, stunting, wasting, underweight, anaemia |
| Health-care delivery | Doctor–population ratio, beds per population, PHC coverage |
| Utilisation | Immunisation coverage, institutional deliveries, contraceptive use |
| Socio-economic | Literacy, per-capita income, housing, safe water access |
| Composite | Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI), Human Development Index (HDI) |

**Important formulas**

- **Crude death rate** = deaths in a year ÷ mid-year population × 1000
- **Infant mortality rate (IMR)** = deaths of infants below 1 year in a year ÷ live births in that year × 1000. IMR is the best single indicator of the health and living standard of a community.
- **Maternal mortality ratio (MMR)** = maternal deaths ÷ live births × 1,00,000
- **Life expectancy at birth** = average number of years a newborn is expected to live if current death rates continue.

**PQLI** combines three things: IMR, life expectancy at age one, and literacy (scale 0–100).
**HDI** (UNDP) combines: a long and healthy life (life expectancy), knowledge (schooling) and a decent standard of living (income per head).

## 1.4 National Health Policy — Indian perspective

A health policy is the government's written plan of goals and the way to reach them.

| Policy | Main ideas |
| --- | --- |
| **NHP 1983** | "Health for All by 2000 AD"; expand primary health care through PHCs and sub-centres; community participation; health volunteers |
| **NHP 2002** | Increase public spending on health; strengthen primary care; decentralise; more role for the private sector; control of TB, malaria, HIV, blindness |
| **NHP 2017** | Highest possible level of health and well-being for all at all ages through preventive and promotive care; universal access to good-quality health care without financial hardship |

**Key features of NHP 2017 (learn these for 5 marks)**

1. Move from "sick care" to **wellness** — preventive and promotive health.
2. **Comprehensive primary care** through Health and Wellness Centres (now Ayushman Arogya Mandirs).
3. **Free essential medicines and diagnostics** in public hospitals.
4. Raise public health spending as a share of GDP in a time-bound way.
5. **Strategic purchasing** of services from the private sector where needed.
6. Focus on non-communicable diseases, mental health, and reducing out-of-pocket spending.
7. Mainstreaming of **AYUSH**; use of digital health (health records).
8. Encourage generic medicines and a strong drug regulatory system.

## 1.5 Public and private health system in India

Health is a **state subject** in the Constitution, but the centre funds national programmes and sets policy.

**Levels of administration:** Union Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW) and Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) → State health departments → District (Chief Medical Officer) → Block → Village.

**Three-tier public health-care delivery**

```text
TERTIARY   Medical colleges, AIIMS, super-speciality hospitals
              ^
SECONDARY  District hospital, sub-district hospital, Community Health Centre (CHC)
              ^
PRIMARY    Primary Health Centre (PHC)
              ^
           Sub-Centre / Health and Wellness Centre  <-- ASHA, Anganwadi worker in the village
```

| Unit | Population covered (plains) | Population covered (hilly/tribal) | Staff and work |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sub-centre | 5,000 | 3,000 | ANM and male health worker; immunisation, ANC, family planning |
| PHC | 30,000 | 20,000 | Medical officer, pharmacist, nurses; curative + preventive care, 4–6 beds |
| CHC | 1,20,000 | 80,000 | Specialists (surgeon, physician, gynaecologist, paediatrician); 30 beds; first referral unit |

These norms matter in Himachal Pradesh, where many areas are hilly, so the lower figures apply.

**Other public systems:** ESI (Employees' State Insurance) hospitals for workers, CGHS for central government employees, railway and defence hospitals, AYUSH hospitals.

**Private sector:** clinics, nursing homes, corporate hospitals, chemists, private labs. It provides a large share of out-patient care in India, but costs are higher and quality varies. NGOs, charitable trusts and voluntary organisations form a third sector.

| Public sector | Private sector |
| --- | --- |
| Free or low cost | Fee for service, often costly |
| Strong in rural preventive care and programmes | Strong in urban curative and specialist care |
| Crowding, staff shortages | Variable regulation and quality |

### National Health Mission (NHM)

- **NRHM** started in 2005 for rural areas; **NUHM** in 2013 for urban poor; both are now sub-missions of **NHM**.
- **Aim:** universal access to equitable, affordable and quality health care that is accountable and responsive to people's needs.

**Main components**

1. Health systems strengthening — infrastructure, staff, free drugs and diagnostics, ambulances (108/102).
2. **RMNCH+A** — reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health.
3. Communicable disease control programmes (TB, malaria, leprosy, etc.).
4. Non-communicable disease control.

**Key features:** ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) in every village; Janani Suraksha Yojana (cash help for institutional delivery); Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (free delivery and care of sick newborns); Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (child screening); Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (adolescents); Rogi Kalyan Samitis (hospital committees); Village Health Sanitation and Nutrition Committees; flexible funds to states.

## 1.6 Development goals

### Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), 2000–2015

Agreed by UN member countries in 2000. Eight goals:

1. Eradicate extreme poverty and hunger
2. Achieve universal primary education
3. Promote gender equality and empower women
4. Reduce child mortality
5. Improve maternal health
6. Combat HIV/AIDS, malaria and other diseases
7. Ensure environmental sustainability
8. Develop a global partnership for development

Goals 4, 5 and 6 are directly health goals.

### Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), 2015–2030

They replaced the MDGs. There are **17 goals** covering poverty, hunger, health, education, gender, water, energy, work, industry, inequality, cities, consumption, climate, life below water, life on land, peace and partnerships.

**SDG 3 — Good health and well-being:** ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages. Its targets include reducing maternal and newborn deaths, ending epidemics of AIDS, TB, malaria and neglected tropical diseases, reducing deaths from non-communicable diseases, preventing substance abuse, reducing road-traffic deaths, universal access to reproductive health care, **universal health coverage** and access to safe, affordable essential medicines and vaccines.

Other health-linked SDGs: SDG 2 (zero hunger), SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation), SDG 5 (gender equality).

| MDGs | SDGs |
| --- | --- |
| 8 goals | 17 goals |
| 2000–2015 | 2015–2030 |
| Mainly for developing countries | Universal — all countries |
| Health in 3 separate goals | One broad health goal (SDG 3) plus links in others |

### FIP Development Goals

FIP (International Pharmaceutical Federation) launched its **Development Goals** in 2020 to transform pharmacy worldwide. They are **21 goals** grouped into three areas:

- **Academy (education):** academic capacity, early-career training, quality assurance of education.
- **Practice (professional services):** people-centred care, antimicrobial stewardship, communicable and non-communicable disease prevention, medicine safety, equity and access to medicines, digital health, sustainability.
- **Workforce:** leadership, competency development, workforce planning, gender and diversity balance.

They link directly to the SDGs and universal health coverage: the pharmacy workforce is seen as a key tool to reach SDG 3.

## Remember

- WHO health definition (1948): complete **physical, mental and social** well-being, not merely absence of disease.
- Six main dimensions: physical, mental, social, spiritual, emotional, vocational.
- IMR = infant deaths < 1 year per 1000 live births; MMR per 1,00,000 live births.
- Sub-centre 5,000 / PHC 30,000 / CHC 1,20,000 (hilly: 3,000 / 20,000 / 80,000).
- NHM = NRHM (2005) + NUHM (2013); ASHA is the village link worker.
- NHP 2017 = wellness, Health and Wellness Centres, free drugs and diagnostics.
- MDGs 8 (2000–2015); SDGs 17 (2015–2030), SDG 3 = health; FIP DGs 21 (2020).

# Unit 2: Preventive Healthcare — Role of Pharmacists

Prevention is cheaper and kinder than cure. This unit covers population and family planning, mother and child health, vaccines, the environment, and drug abuse — and what a pharmacist does in each.

**Levels of prevention (useful opening for any long answer)**

| Level | When | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primordial | Before risk factors appear | Healthy lifestyle habits in children |
| Primary | Before disease starts | Vaccination, safe water, condoms, health education |
| Secondary | Early disease | Screening for BP, diabetes, TB; early treatment |
| Tertiary | Established disease | Rehabilitation, limiting disability (e.g. leprosy care) |

## 2.1 Demography and family planning

### Demography

**Demography** is the scientific study of human population: its **size, composition (age, sex), distribution, and changes** caused by births, deaths and migration.

**Sources of data:** Census (every 10 years in India), Sample Registration System (SRS), National Family Health Survey (NFHS), civil registration of births and deaths.

**Demographic cycle (five stages)**

```text
Stage 1 High stationary   High birth rate, high death rate     -> slow growth
Stage 2 Early expanding   Death rate falls, birth rate high    -> fast growth
Stage 3 Late expanding    Birth rate starts falling            -> growth slows
Stage 4 Low stationary    Low birth rate, low death rate       -> stable
Stage 5 Declining         Birth rate below death rate          -> population falls
```

India is generally placed in the **late expanding** stage.

**Demographic indicators**

| Indicator | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Crude birth rate | Live births per 1000 mid-year population per year |
| Crude death rate | Deaths per 1000 mid-year population per year |
| Growth rate | Birth rate minus death rate (plus migration) |
| Total fertility rate (TFR) | Average children a woman would have in her reproductive life; 2.1 = replacement level |
| Sex ratio (India) | Females per 1000 males |
| Dependency ratio | Children (0–14) + elderly (65+) per 100 working-age people (15–64) |

**Problems of a fast-growing population:** pressure on food, water, housing, schools and jobs; unemployment; poor health services; environmental damage; poverty.

### Family planning

WHO describes family planning as a way of thinking and living adopted voluntarily, based on knowledge and responsible decisions, to promote the health of the family. It lets couples decide **how many children to have and when**.

**Benefits:** spacing between births (healthier mother and child), fewer unsafe abortions, lower maternal and infant deaths, better nutrition and education for children, control of population growth.

**Classification of contraceptive methods**

```text
CONTRACEPTIVES
├── Spacing (temporary)
│   ├── Barrier: condom (male/female), diaphragm, spermicides
│   ├── Intra-uterine devices (IUD): Cu-T 380A, Cu-T 375, LNG-IUS
│   ├── Hormonal: oral pills, injectables, implants, emergency pill
│   ├── Non-hormonal pill: centchroman
│   └── Natural: rhythm/calendar, withdrawal, LAM (breastfeeding)
└── Terminal (permanent)
    ├── Male: vasectomy (no-scalpel vasectomy)
    └── Female: tubectomy (laparoscopic / minilap)
```

| Method | How it works | Points for counselling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Male condom | Barrier to sperm | Also protects against STDs/HIV; new one each time |
| Combined oral pill (e.g. Mala-N) | Oestrogen + progestin stop ovulation | One pill daily; 21 hormone + 7 iron tablets; missed pill rules |
| Centchroman (Chhaya) | Non-steroidal; prevents implantation | Twice a week for 3 months, then once a week |
| Injectable DMPA (Antara) | Progestin; stops ovulation | One injection every 3 months; irregular bleeding |
| Cu-T 380A | Copper is toxic to sperm, prevents implantation | Effective for about 10 years; Cu-T 375 about 5 years |
| Emergency pill (levonorgestrel 1.5 mg) | Delays ovulation | Within 72 hours of unprotected sex; not a regular method |
| LAM | Exclusive breastfeeding suppresses ovulation | Only if baby < 6 months, exclusive feeding, no periods |
| Vasectomy / tubectomy | Vas deferens / fallopian tubes cut and tied | Permanent; vasectomy is simpler and safer |

**Role of pharmacist:** stock and explain methods; explain missed-pill rules; tell clients that the emergency pill is not for regular use; promote condoms for dual protection; maintain privacy; refer for IUD or sterilisation; support national campaigns.

## 2.2 Mother and child health (MCH)

Mothers and children form a large, vulnerable group. Most maternal and infant deaths are preventable.

**Antenatal care (ANC)**

- Early registration, at least four ANC visits.
- Tetanus–diphtheria (Td) vaccine, two doses (or one booster).
- Iron–folic acid tablets daily from the second trimester; calcium; deworming after the first trimester.
- Check weight, BP, haemoglobin, urine, blood sugar; identify high-risk pregnancy (anaemia, high BP, previous caesarean, twins).
- Advice on diet, rest, danger signs (bleeding, fits, swelling, reduced foetal movement).

**Intranatal care:** institutional delivery by skilled birth attendant; "five cleans" if delivered at home (clean hands, surface, blade, cord tie, cord stump).
**Postnatal care:** check mother and baby, breastfeeding support, family planning advice, newborn immunisation.

### Importance of breastfeeding

**Recommendations:** start within **one hour** of birth; give **colostrum** (first thick yellow milk); **exclusive** breastfeeding for the first **6 months** (no water, honey, ghutti); then add complementary foods and continue breastfeeding up to **2 years** or beyond.

| Benefits to baby | Benefits to mother | Benefits to family/society |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Perfect nutrition, easy to digest | Less bleeding after delivery (uterus contracts) | Free, always ready, no preparation |
| Antibodies (IgA in colostrum) protect against diarrhoea and pneumonia | Natural spacing (LAM) | No fuel, bottles or water needed |
| Lower risk of allergy, obesity, diabetes later | Lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer | Fewer illnesses, lower health costs |
| Better brain development, bonding | Faster return to pre-pregnancy weight | Environment-friendly |

### Ill effects of infant milk substitutes and bottle feeding

- **Infections:** bottles and teats are hard to clean → diarrhoea, thrush.
- **Over-dilution** (to save money) → malnutrition, marasmus; **under-dilution** → dehydration, kidney load, obesity.
- No antibodies → more pneumonia and ear infections.
- Allergy to cow's milk protein; poorer bonding.
- Costly; needs safe water and fuel.
- Mother loses natural contraception.

India's **Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods Act (IMS Act), 1992**, amended in 2003, bans advertising and promotion of infant milk substitutes and feeding bottles, so that breastfeeding is protected.

**Role of pharmacist:** do not promote formula; counsel mothers on breastfeeding and correct expressing/storage of breast milk; explain safe preparation if formula is medically needed; supply ORS and zinc; check immunisation card.

## 2.3 Vaccines, immunity and immunisation

### Immunity

**Immunity** is the body's ability to resist infection.

```text
IMMUNITY
├── Innate (non-specific): skin, mucus, stomach acid, phagocytes, fever
└── Acquired (specific)
    ├── Active (body makes its own antibodies; slow onset, long-lasting)
    │   ├── Natural: after an infection (e.g. measles)
    │   └── Artificial: after a vaccine
    └── Passive (ready-made antibodies; quick, short-lived)
        ├── Natural: mother → baby via placenta and breast milk
        └── Artificial: immunoglobulins, antitoxins, antisera (e.g. anti-rabies Ig, ASV)
```

**Herd immunity:** when most of a community is immune, the infection cannot spread easily, so even unvaccinated people are protected.

### Types of vaccines

| Type | Description | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Live attenuated | Weakened live organism; strong, long immunity; avoid in pregnancy and immunodeficiency | BCG, OPV, measles–rubella (MR), rotavirus, varicella, yellow fever |
| Inactivated (killed) | Whole killed organism; needs boosters | IPV, rabies cell-culture vaccine, hepatitis A, whole-cell pertussis |
| Toxoid | Inactivated toxin | Tetanus, diphtheria |
| Subunit / recombinant | Only a part (protein) of the microbe | Hepatitis B, HPV, acellular pertussis |
| Conjugate | Sugar coat joined to a protein for better response in infants | Hib, pneumococcal (PCV), typhoid conjugate |
| mRNA / viral vector (newer) | Carry instructions to make an antigen | Some COVID-19 vaccines |

### Immunisation in India

The **Universal Immunization Programme (UIP)** gives free vaccines to children and pregnant women. **Mission Indradhanush** catches up children and women who missed doses. The full schedule is in the practical "National immunization schedule".

**Cold chain** — the system of keeping vaccines at the right temperature from maker to child.

- Most vaccines: **+2 °C to +8 °C**; never freeze Td, pentavalent, hepatitis B, PCV.
- Equipment: walk-in coolers, ice-lined refrigerators (ILR), deep freezers, cold boxes, vaccine carriers with ice packs.
- **Vaccine vial monitor (VVM):** a square inside a circle on the label; if the square becomes as dark as or darker than the circle, the vaccine has had too much heat — discard.
- **Shake test:** checks whether a freeze-sensitive vaccine has been frozen.
- OPV is the most heat-sensitive; BCG and MR must be protected from light.

**Adverse events following immunisation (AEFI):** mild (fever, pain, swelling) to rare serious ones (anaphylaxis). Every AEFI must be reported.

**Role of pharmacist:** explain the schedule and remind about due doses; maintain the cold chain where vaccines are stocked; counsel about mild side effects (paracetamol for fever); dispel myths; report AEFI; promote adult vaccines (influenza, hepatitis B).

## 2.4 Effect of environment on health

### Water pollution and safe drinking water

**Safe and wholesome water** is free from pathogens and harmful chemicals, pleasant to taste, and usable for domestic purposes.

**Sources of pollution:** sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural run-off (fertilisers, pesticides), animal waste, hospital waste.

**Water-borne and water-related diseases**

| Group | Diseases |
| --- | --- |
| Viral | Hepatitis A and E, poliomyelitis, rotavirus diarrhoea |
| Bacterial | Cholera, typhoid, bacillary dysentery, E. coli diarrhoea |
| Protozoal | Amoebiasis, giardiasis |
| Helminthic | Roundworm, threadworm, guinea worm (now eradicated in India) |
| Chemical | Fluorosis (excess fluoride), arsenic poisoning, nitrate excess (blue-baby), lead |

**Purification of water**

- **Large scale:** storage → filtration (slow sand or rapid sand filters) → chlorination.
- **Small scale (household):** boiling (rolling boil for 5–10 minutes), chlorination (bleaching powder, chlorine tablets), filtration (ceramic filters), ultraviolet and reverse-osmosis units.
- **Chlorination rule:** after a contact period of 1 hour, a **free residual chlorine of 0.5 mg/L** should remain. Bleaching powder contains about **33% available chlorine**.

### Air pollution

**Main pollutants:** particulate matter (PM10, PM2.5), carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, ozone, lead, smoke. **Indoor pollution:** smoke from wood, cow-dung cakes and kerosene in poorly ventilated kitchens; tobacco smoke.

**Health effects:** asthma, chronic bronchitis, COPD, lung cancer, heart disease, eye irritation; CO binds haemoglobin and reduces oxygen delivery.

**Control:** clean fuels (LPG), better stoves and ventilation, vehicle emission norms, industrial filters, tree planting, masks on high-pollution days.

### Noise pollution

Unwanted sound, measured in **decibels (dB)**. Long exposure above about **85 dB** damages hearing.
**Effects:** noise-induced hearing loss, annoyance, poor sleep, high BP, poor concentration.
**Control:** silencers, sound barriers, ear plugs and muffs, limits on loudspeakers and horns.

### Sewage and solid waste disposal

**Sewage** = waste water from houses and industries. Treatment: primary (screening, grit removal, sedimentation) → secondary (biological: activated sludge, trickling filters, oxidation ponds) → (tertiary in some plants) → safe discharge. Rural options: sanitary latrines (pour-flush, two-pit), septic tanks. **Swachh Bharat Mission** promotes toilets and ending open defecation.

**Solid waste (refuse):** methods — composting, sanitary landfill, incineration, recycling; segregate at source into wet (green bin) and dry (blue bin).

**Bio-medical waste (BMW Management Rules, 2016) colour coding**

| Colour | Waste | Treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yellow | Anatomical waste, soiled dressings, expired or discarded medicines, chemical waste | Incineration / deep burial |
| Red | Contaminated recyclable plastics: tubing, catheters, IV sets, syringes without needles, gloves | Autoclave/microwave, then recycling |
| White (translucent, puncture-proof) | Sharps: needles, blades, scalpels | Autoclave, shredding |
| Blue | Glassware, broken or discarded glass, metal implants | Disinfection, then recycling |

### Occupational illnesses

Diseases caused by the work environment.

| Hazard | Disease / example |
| --- | --- |
| Dusts | Pneumoconioses: silicosis (silica, mining, stone-cutting), asbestosis, anthracosis (coal), byssinosis (cotton), bagassosis (sugarcane), farmer's lung |
| Chemicals | Lead poisoning, mercury poisoning, benzene (leukaemia), occupational dermatitis |
| Physical | Noise-induced deafness, heat stroke, radiation injury |
| Biological | Anthrax, brucellosis, hepatitis B and needle-stick injuries in health workers |
| Mechanical/ergonomic | Back pain, accidents, repetitive strain |
| Psychosocial | Stress, shift-work problems |

**Prevention:** engineering controls (ventilation, enclosure, wet drilling), protective equipment, pre-placement and periodic medical examination, health education. Laws: **Factories Act 1948**, **ESI Act 1948**.

### Environmental pollution due to pharmaceuticals

Medicines enter the environment from **factory effluents**, **hospital waste**, excretion by people and animals, and **wrong disposal** (flushing or throwing in garbage).

**Problems:**

- Antibiotic residues → **antimicrobial resistance** in environmental bacteria.
- Hormones such as ethinyl-oestradiol → feminisation of fish.
- Veterinary **diclofenac** in cattle carcasses caused a steep fall in India's vulture population; its veterinary use was banned.
- Contamination of drinking water and soil.

**Prevention and role of pharmacist:** effluent treatment plants in industry; green chemistry; take-back of unused and expired medicines; proper BMW segregation; never flush medicines; prescribe and dispense only needed quantities; educate the public.

## 2.5 Psychosocial pharmacy: drugs of misuse and abuse

**Definitions**

- **Drug misuse:** use of a medicine for a purpose or in a way not intended (e.g. extra sleeping pills).
- **Drug abuse:** self-administration of a drug, usually for pleasure, in a way that harms health or social life.
- **Tolerance:** larger doses needed for the same effect.
- **Dependence:** psychological (craving) and/or physical (withdrawal symptoms when stopped).
- **Addiction:** compulsive use despite harm.

| Class | Examples | Main dangers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opioids (narcotics) | Morphine, heroin (smack), codeine syrups, tramadol | Respiratory depression, overdose death, HIV/hepatitis by shared needles |
| CNS depressants | Alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates | Accidents, dependence, dangerous withdrawal |
| Stimulants | Cocaine, amphetamines | Psychosis, heart attack, stroke |
| Cannabis | Bhang, ganja, charas | Impaired memory, psychosis |
| Hallucinogens | LSD | Bad trips, accidents |
| Inhalants | Glue, solvents, whitener | Brain and liver damage, sudden death |
| Tobacco | Cigarettes, bidi, gutkha, khaini | Cancer, heart and lung disease |

**Law:** Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985.

**Alcohol:** acute — intoxication, accidents, violence; chronic — fatty liver, cirrhosis, pancreatitis, gastritis, thiamine deficiency (Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome), depression, family breakdown. Withdrawal — tremors, sweating, fits, delirium tremens. Treatment — detoxification with benzodiazepines plus thiamine; relapse prevention with disulfiram, naltrexone or acamprosate; counselling, self-help groups.

**Tobacco:** nicotine is the addictive substance. Causes oral, lung and throat cancers, heart attacks, stroke, COPD, low birth weight. Smokeless tobacco is common in India. **COTPA, 2003** bans smoking in public places, sale to minors and sale within 100 yards of educational institutions, and requires pictorial warnings. Help to quit: counselling (5 As and 5 Rs), nicotine replacement (gum, patch, lozenge), bupropion, varenicline.

**Social impact of these habits:** poor school and work performance, absenteeism and loss of productivity, poverty from spending on drugs, crime and violence, road accidents, family disputes and domestic violence, spread of HIV and hepatitis, stigma.

**Suicidal behaviour:** substance abuse, depression, chronic illness, debt, exam stress and family problems raise the risk. Warning signs: talking about death, giving away belongings, withdrawal from friends, buying large amounts of tablets or pesticides. Pharmacist role: notice repeated purchase of sedatives, listen without judging, refer to a doctor or the national tele-mental health helpline (**Tele-MANAS, 14416**), support safe storage of pesticides and medicines.

**Means to avoid substance abuse (role of pharmacist)**

1. Sell schedule H, H1 and X drugs and codeine syrups only on valid prescription; keep records.
2. Watch for repeated purchases and "doctor shopping".
3. Educate schools and youth about harms; use posters and talks.
4. Counsel smokers and drinkers to quit; supply nicotine replacement.
5. Refer to de-addiction centres; support families.
6. Report suspicious activity; follow the NDPS Act.

## Remember

- Demographic cycle has 5 stages; India is in the late expanding stage. Replacement TFR = 2.1.
- Cu-T 380A ≈ 10 years; Chhaya = centchroman, weekly after the first 3 months; Antara = DMPA every 3 months; emergency pill within 72 h.
- Breastfeed within 1 hour, exclusive 6 months, continue to 2 years; IMS Act 1992.
- Live vaccines: BCG, OPV, MR, rotavirus. Toxoids: tetanus, diphtheria. Cold chain +2 to +8 °C; VVM tells heat exposure.
- Residual chlorine 0.5 mg/L after 1 hour; bleaching powder ≈ 33% available chlorine.
- BMW 2016: yellow, red, white (sharps), blue (glass).
- NDPS Act 1985; COTPA 2003; Tele-MANAS 14416.
