# Unit 3: Nutrition and Health

**Nutrition** is the science of food and how the body uses it for growth, energy, repair and protection from disease. Good nutrition is the base of health; poor nutrition (too little or too much) underlies anaemia, stunting, obesity, diabetes and heart disease.

## 3.1 Basics of nutrition — macronutrients and micronutrients

**Nutrients** are substances in food that the body needs.

```text
NUTRIENTS
├── Macronutrients (needed in grams; give energy or build tissue)
│   ├── Carbohydrates  4 kcal/g
│   ├── Proteins       4 kcal/g
│   └── Fats           9 kcal/g
├── Micronutrients (needed in mg or µg; no energy)
│   ├── Vitamins: fat-soluble A, D, E, K; water-soluble B-complex, C
│   └── Minerals: calcium, iron, iodine, zinc, sodium, potassium, fluoride ...
└── Water and dietary fibre
```

(Alcohol also gives about 7 kcal/g, but it is not a nutrient.)

### Carbohydrates

- **Function:** main and cheapest source of energy; spare protein; brain uses glucose.
- **Types:** simple sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose, lactose) and complex carbohydrates (starch in rice, wheat, potato; fibre).
- **Sources:** cereals, millets, roots and tubers, sugar, jaggery, fruits.
- Excess refined sugar → obesity, dental caries, diabetes risk.

### Proteins

- **Function:** body-building (muscle, enzymes, hormones, antibodies, haemoglobin), repair, growth.
- Made of **amino acids**; 9 are **essential** (must come from food) for adults (e.g. lysine, tryptophan, methionine, leucine).
- **Quality:** animal proteins (milk, egg, meat, fish) are complete; most plant proteins lack one amino acid. Cereals lack lysine, pulses lack methionine — so **cereal + pulse** (dal-roti, khichdi, rajma-chawal) gives good-quality protein ("supplementary action").
- **Sources:** pulses, soya, milk, curd, paneer, egg, meat, fish, groundnuts.

### Fats (lipids)

- **Function:** concentrated energy, carry fat-soluble vitamins, essential fatty acids, insulation, taste.
- **Types:** saturated (ghee, butter, coconut oil), monounsaturated (groundnut, mustard, olive oil), polyunsaturated — omega-6 (sunflower, safflower) and omega-3 (fish, flaxseed, mustard). **Trans fats** (vanaspati, repeatedly heated oil, bakery foods) raise heart-disease risk.
- **Essential fatty acids:** linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid.
- Excess fat → obesity, high cholesterol, heart disease.

### Vitamins

| Vitamin | Main sources | Deficiency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A (retinol) | Liver, milk, egg yolk, green leafy and yellow vegetables, papaya, mango (β-carotene) | Night blindness, Bitot's spots, xerophthalmia, keratomalacia (blindness) |
| D | Sunlight on skin, fish oils, egg, fortified milk | Rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults |
| E | Vegetable oils, nuts, seeds | Haemolysis, nerve problems (rare) |
| K | Green leafy vegetables, gut bacteria | Bleeding; haemorrhagic disease of newborn |
| B1 (thiamine) | Whole grains, pulses, unpolished rice | Beriberi (wet: heart failure; dry: neuritis); Wernicke's in alcoholics |
| B2 (riboflavin) | Milk, egg, green leaves | Angular stomatitis, cheilosis, glossitis |
| B3 (niacin) | Groundnut, meat, cereals | Pellagra: 3 Ds — dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia (4th D = death) |
| B6 (pyridoxine) | Cereals, meat, banana | Peripheral neuritis (e.g. with isoniazid), convulsions in infants |
| Folic acid | Green leafy vegetables, liver, pulses | Megaloblastic anaemia; neural tube defects in foetus |
| B12 | Only animal foods: milk, meat, egg | Megaloblastic anaemia, nerve damage (vegetarians at risk) |
| C (ascorbic acid) | Amla, citrus fruits, guava, tomato | Scurvy: bleeding gums, poor wound healing |

### Minerals

| Mineral | Role | Sources | Deficiency / excess |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Iron | Haemoglobin | Green leaves, jaggery, meat, liver, pulses (vitamin C helps absorption) | Microcytic hypochromic anaemia, tiredness, poor learning |
| Calcium | Bones, teeth, muscle, clotting | Milk, curd, ragi, sesame | Rickets, osteoporosis |
| Iodine | Thyroid hormones | Iodised salt, sea food | Goitre, cretinism, mental retardation (IDD) |
| Zinc | Growth, immunity, wound healing | Meat, pulses, nuts | Growth failure, diarrhoea |
| Fluoride | Teeth | Water, tea | Too little → dental caries; too much → dental and skeletal fluorosis |
| Sodium | Fluid balance | Salt | Excess → high BP |

## 3.2 Importance of water and fibre in the diet

### Water

- About **60% of adult body weight** is water.
- Functions: solvent and transport medium, temperature control (sweat), digestion, kidney excretion of waste, joint lubrication.
- Need: roughly 2–3 litres a day for an adult, more in heat, exercise, fever, diarrhoea, pregnancy and lactation.
- **Dehydration** → thirst, dry mouth, low urine, dizziness, kidney stones, constipation; severe dehydration (e.g. cholera) can kill.

### Dietary fibre

The part of plant food that human enzymes cannot digest.

| Type | Examples | Benefits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Soluble | Oats, pulses, isabgol (psyllium husk), apples, guar gum | Lowers blood cholesterol, slows sugar absorption (good in diabetes) |
| Insoluble | Wheat bran, whole grains, vegetables, fruit peels | Adds bulk, prevents constipation, piles and diverticulosis |

Fibre also gives a feeling of fullness (helps weight control) and feeds good gut bacteria. Too little fibre is linked with constipation and colon cancer. Increase fibre slowly and drink enough water.

## 3.3 Balanced diet, malnutrition and deficiency diseases

### Balanced diet

A **balanced diet** contains all nutrients in the right amounts and proportions to meet the body's needs, keep a small reserve, and maintain health.

**Approximate share of energy:** carbohydrates about 50–60%, proteins 10–15%, fats 20–30%.

**Food groups (ICMR–NIN idea)**

| Group | Foods | Main nutrients |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cereals and millets | Rice, wheat, ragi, bajra, maize | Energy, some protein, B vitamins |
| Pulses and legumes | Dals, beans, soya | Protein, iron, fibre |
| Milk and animal foods | Milk, curd, egg, meat, fish | High-quality protein, calcium, B12 |
| Vegetables and fruits | Green leaves, other vegetables, seasonal fruits | Vitamins A and C, minerals, fibre |
| Fats, oils, nuts and sugar | Oil, ghee, nuts, sugar, jaggery | Energy, essential fatty acids |

**Practical tips:** half the plate vegetables and fruits; whole grains and millets; dal or an animal protein every meal; limit salt (WHO advises below 5 g a day), sugar and fried food; drink enough water; eat at regular times.

**Special groups:** pregnant women need extra energy, protein, iron, folic acid and calcium; lactating women need extra energy and protein; growing children need more protein and calcium per kg; elderly people need less energy but enough protein, calcium and vitamin D.

### Malnutrition

**Malnutrition** means an imbalance of nutrients — both **undernutrition** (too little) and **overnutrition** (too much).

**Causes:** poverty, food insecurity, large families, poor feeding practices, infections (diarrhoea, worms), lack of education, low status of women, poor sanitation.

**Protein–energy malnutrition (PEM)** in young children:

| Feature | Marasmus | Kwashiorkor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main deficit | Energy (and protein) | Mainly protein |
| Age | Usually under 1 year | 1–3 years (after weaning) |
| Oedema | Absent | Present (feet, face) |
| Look | "Old man" face, skin and bones, severe wasting | Puffy, "moon" face, flaky-paint skin |
| Hair | Thin | Sparse, pale or reddish (hence "red boy"), easily pulled out |
| Liver | Normal | Fatty, enlarged |
| Appetite | Good | Poor, apathetic, irritable |

**Measurements:** stunting (low height for age — long-term undernutrition), wasting (low weight for height — recent undernutrition), underweight (low weight for age), mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC).

**Overnutrition:** obesity (BMI ≥ 25 kg/m² is overweight on WHO cut-offs; Asian Indians face risk at lower BMI), type 2 diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, some cancers.
**BMI** = weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²).

### Nutrition deficiency diseases (summary)

PEM; vitamin A deficiency; iron-deficiency anaemia (the commonest nutritional problem in India); iodine deficiency disorders; rickets and osteomalacia; beriberi; pellagra; scurvy; megaloblastic anaemia; zinc deficiency.

**Control programmes:** ICDS (Anganwadi services), PM POSHAN (school mid-day meal), POSHAN Abhiyaan, Anemia Mukt Bharat, vitamin A supplementation, National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme.

### Ill effects of junk foods

**Junk food** = food high in calories, salt, sugar or unhealthy fat but low in protein, vitamins, minerals and fibre (chips, instant noodles, fried snacks, sugary soft drinks, burgers, pastries). Also called HFSS (high fat, salt, sugar) food.

**Ill effects:**

- Obesity, especially in children and teenagers.
- Type 2 diabetes, high BP, high cholesterol and early heart disease.
- Dental caries (sugar), acidity, constipation (no fibre).
- Poor concentration, tiredness, mood swings; displaces healthy food → micronutrient deficiency.
- Some additives, colours and repeatedly heated oils may be harmful.

### Calorific and nutritive values of foods

**Calorific value** = energy given by a food, in kilocalories (kcal) per 100 g. **Nutritive value** = its content of protein, fat, vitamins and minerals.

Approximate values per 100 g (edible portion):

| Food | Energy (kcal, approx.) | Notable nutrient |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rice (raw) | 345 | Carbohydrate |
| Wheat flour (atta) | 340 | Carbohydrate, some protein |
| Pulses (dal, raw) | 330–350 | Protein about 20–24 g |
| Groundnuts | 560–570 | Fat, protein |
| Cow's milk | 65–70 | Calcium, protein |
| Egg (one, about 50 g) | 70–80 | High-quality protein |
| Sugar | 400 | Only carbohydrate ("empty calories") |
| Cooking oil | 900 | Only fat |
| Green leafy vegetables | 30–50 | Iron, β-carotene, folic acid |
| Amla | 50–60 | Very rich in vitamin C |

**Calculating energy from a label:** energy (kcal) = 4 × carbohydrate (g) + 4 × protein (g) + 9 × fat (g).
*Example:* a snack with 20 g carbohydrate, 2 g protein and 10 g fat gives 80 + 8 + 90 = 178 kcal.

### Fortification of food

**Fortification** = adding vitamins or minerals to commonly eaten foods to prevent deficiency in the whole population, without changing eating habits.

| Food vehicle | Nutrient added | Prevents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Salt | Iodine (iodised salt); iodine + iron (double-fortified salt) | IDD, anaemia |
| Rice | Iron, folic acid, vitamin B12 (fortified rice kernels) | Anaemia |
| Wheat flour | Iron, folic acid, B12 | Anaemia |
| Edible oil | Vitamins A and D | Vitamin A and D deficiency |
| Milk | Vitamins A and D | Vitamin A and D deficiency |

FSSAI marks fortified foods with the **"+F" logo**. Other terms: **enrichment** (adding back nutrients lost in processing) and **biofortification** (breeding crops richer in nutrients, e.g. iron-rich pearl millet).

## 3.4 Food safety

**Food safety** means food will not harm the consumer when prepared and eaten as intended. In India the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006** is enforced by **FSSAI** (Food Safety and Standards Authority of India).

**Five keys to safer food (WHO):** keep clean; separate raw and cooked food; cook thoroughly; keep food at safe temperatures; use safe water and raw materials.

### Adulteration of foods

**Adulteration** = adding cheaper or harmful substances, removing valuable parts, or selling spoiled food as good.

| Food | Common adulterant | Harm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Milk | Water, starch, urea, detergent | Low nutrition, gut and kidney harm |
| Ghee/butter | Vanaspati, animal fat | Heart disease risk |
| Mustard oil | Argemone oil | Epidemic dropsy (oedema, heart failure, glaucoma) |
| Arhar dal | Khesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) | Lathyrism (paralysis of legs) |
| Turmeric | Metanil yellow, lead chromate | Toxic, possibly cancer-causing |
| Chilli powder | Brick powder, artificial colours | Gut irritation, toxicity |
| Black pepper | Dried papaya seeds | Fraud, low quality |
| Tea | Used tea leaves, colour | Liver harm (from colour) |
| Coffee | Chicory, tamarind seed powder | Fraud |
| Sweets | Non-permitted colours, aluminium foil instead of silver | Toxicity |

**Simple home tests:** a drop of iodine turns starch-adulterated milk or paneer blue; papaya seeds float in spirit while true pepper sinks; brick powder in chilli settles quickly in water.

### Effects of artificial ripening

Fruits such as mango, banana and papaya are sometimes ripened quickly with **calcium carbide**. With moisture it gives **acetylene** gas; industrial carbide also carries traces of **arsenic and phosphorus**.

**Effects:** headache, dizziness, vomiting, burning and ulcers in mouth and stomach, skin and eye irritation; long-term toxicity. Fruit looks ripe outside but is raw and tasteless inside. Calcium carbide use is **banned** under FSSAI rules; controlled **ethylene gas** ripening chambers are the permitted method.

**Signs of carbide-ripened fruit:** patchy colour (yellow skin with green patches), uniform colour all over a batch, bland taste, quick spoilage. Advice: wash fruit well, peel, buy seasonal fruit.

### Use of pesticides

Pesticides (insecticides, herbicides, fungicides) protect crops but residues in food can harm health.

**Problems:** acute poisoning (organophosphates), residues in vegetables, fruits and milk; long-term effects on nerves, hormones and possibly cancer; harm to bees and birds; resistance in pests.

**Control:** maximum residue limits (MRL) set by FSSAI; banning of dangerous pesticides; integrated pest management; organic farming. **Home advice:** wash vegetables and fruits well in running water (soaking in salt water helps), peel where possible, cook.

### Genetically modified (GM) foods

GM foods come from organisms whose DNA has been changed by genetic engineering to add a useful trait.

| Possible benefits | Concerns |
| --- | --- |
| Pest resistance (e.g. Bt cotton), less pesticide use | Allergy to new proteins |
| Higher yield, drought or salt tolerance | Gene flow to wild plants, loss of biodiversity |
| Better nutrition (e.g. "golden rice" with β-carotene) | Resistance in pests over time |
| Longer shelf life | Dependence on seed companies; labelling and ethics |

In India, GM crops need approval of the **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)**; Bt cotton is the main GM crop grown commercially, and GM food crops remain tightly controlled.

## 3.5 Dietary supplements, nutraceuticals and drug–food interactions

**Dietary (food) supplement:** a product taken by mouth to add to the diet (vitamins, minerals, proteins, herbs), usually as tablets, capsules, powders or liquids.

**Nutraceutical:** a food or part of a food that gives medical or health benefits, including prevention and support in disease (word made from *nutrition* + *pharmaceutical*). In India these are regulated by FSSAI, not as drugs.

| Product | Indications / benefits |
| --- | --- |
| Iron + folic acid, calcium + vitamin D | Anaemia in pregnancy; bone health, osteoporosis |
| Multivitamin–multimineral | Poor diet, recovery from illness, elderly |
| Omega-3 fatty acids (fish oil, flaxseed) | Lowering triglycerides, heart health |
| Probiotics (Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium) | Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, gut health |
| Prebiotics (inulin, FOS) | Feed good gut bacteria |
| Protein powders | Undernutrition, elderly, athletes, recovery after surgery |
| Glucosamine, chondroitin | Joint pain in osteoarthritis (evidence is mixed) |
| Antioxidants (vitamins C, E, lycopene) | General wellness claims |
| Psyllium (isabgol) | Constipation, cholesterol |

**Pharmacist's caution:** supplements are not a substitute for a balanced diet; overdose is possible (vitamin A and D toxicity, iron poisoning in children); some interact with drugs; check quality and FSSAI licence; avoid unproven claims.

### Drug–food interactions

A **drug–food interaction** is a change in a drug's effect because of food or drink taken with it.

| Food / drink | Drug | Result | Advice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Milk, dairy, antacids, iron | Tetracyclines, ciprofloxacin | Chelation → less absorption | Gap of 2 hours |
| Grapefruit juice | Felodipine, simvastatin, some others | Blocks gut CYP3A4 → higher blood levels | Avoid grapefruit |
| Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, fermented foods, some wines) | MAO inhibitors | Hypertensive crisis | Avoid such foods |
| Green leafy vegetables (vitamin K) | Warfarin | Lower anticoagulant effect | Keep vitamin K intake steady |
| Alcohol | Metronidazole | Disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, vomiting) | No alcohol during and 2 days after |
| Alcohol | Sedatives, antihistamines, paracetamol (liver) | More sedation; liver damage | Avoid alcohol |
| High-protein meal | Levodopa | Amino acids compete for absorption into brain | Spread protein intake |
| Fatty meal | Griseofulvin | Better absorption | Take with fatty food |
| Food in general | Rifampicin, levothyroxine, alendronate | Less absorption | Take on empty stomach |
| Caffeine | Theophylline | Additive stimulation | Limit tea and coffee |
| Bananas, salt substitutes (potassium) | ACE inhibitors, spironolactone | High potassium | Avoid excess |

**Role of pharmacist:** tell patients clearly "before food / after food / empty stomach"; warn about alcohol; counsel patients on warfarin and MAOIs; check supplements the patient is already taking.

## Remember

- Energy: carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal/g; fats carry vitamins A, D, E, K.
- Cereal + pulse together supply all essential amino acids.
- Kwashiorkor = oedema, "red boy" hair, fatty liver; marasmus = wasting, no oedema.
- Pellagra 3 Ds; scurvy = vitamin C; beriberi = B1; night blindness = vitamin A.
- Argemone oil → epidemic dropsy; khesari dal → lathyrism; metanil yellow in turmeric.
- Calcium carbide (acetylene, arsenic traces) is banned for ripening; ethylene is allowed.
- FSS Act 2006, FSSAI; "+F" logo for fortified foods.
- Classic drug–food pairs: tetracycline + milk, MAOI + cheese, warfarin + green leaves, metronidazole + alcohol.

# Unit 4: Introduction to Microbiology, Epidemiology and Communicable Diseases

This is the heaviest unit of the syllabus (about 28 of the 75 hours). Learn it disease by disease using one fixed format: **agent → spread → incubation → clinical features → prevention → pharmacist's role.**

## 4.1 Introduction to microbiology and common micro-organisms

**Microbiology** is the study of living things too small to be seen without a microscope (micro-organisms or microbes). Most microbes are harmless or useful (curd, fermentation, gut flora, antibiotics production). A few cause disease; these are **pathogens**.

| Group | Size and structure | Examples of diseases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bacteria | Single-celled, no nucleus (prokaryotes), 0.5–5 µm, cell wall | TB, typhoid, cholera, tetanus, diphtheria |
| Viruses | Smallest (20–300 nm); DNA or RNA in a protein coat; grow only inside living cells | Measles, polio, influenza, HIV, dengue, COVID-19 |
| Fungi | Yeasts (single cells) and moulds (threads called hyphae) | Ringworm, oral thrush (Candida) |
| Protozoa | Single-celled animals with a nucleus | Malaria, amoebiasis, giardiasis, kala-azar |
| Helminths | Many-celled worms | Roundworm, hookworm, tapeworm, filaria |
| Rickettsia, Chlamydia | Very small bacteria that live inside cells | Typhus, trachoma |

**Shapes of bacteria**

```text
Cocci (round)      o  oo  oooo (chains: Streptococcus)   cluster (Staphylococcus)
Bacilli (rods)     ===  ===  (E. coli, Salmonella, Mycobacterium)
Vibrio (comma)     (  (  (  (Vibrio cholerae)
Spirochaetes       ~~~~~  (Treponema of syphilis)
```

**Gram stain** divides bacteria into **Gram-positive** (thick cell wall, stain purple/violet — Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Clostridium, Corynebacterium) and **Gram-negative** (thin wall with outer membrane, stain pink/red — E. coli, Salmonella, Vibrio, Neisseria). Mycobacteria are **acid-fast** (Ziehl–Neelsen stain shows red rods).

## 4.2 Epidemiology

**Epidemiology** is the study of the **distribution** (who, where, when) and **determinants** (why) of health-related states in populations, and the use of this study to **control** health problems.

**Applications of epidemiology**

1. Finding the cause and risk factors of a disease (e.g. smoking and lung cancer).
2. Measuring the burden of disease in a community (incidence, prevalence).
3. Studying the natural history of disease.
4. Planning and evaluating health services and national programmes.
5. Investigating outbreaks and controlling them.
6. Testing new vaccines and drugs (clinical trials).
7. Identifying high-risk groups for screening.

**Epidemiological triad**

```text
             AGENT (microbe, toxin)
              /            \
             /   DISEASE    \
            /                \
        HOST ---------------- ENVIRONMENT
 (age, immunity,          (water, climate,
  nutrition, habits)       vectors, crowding)
```

**Chain of infection:** reservoir/source → portal of exit → mode of transmission → portal of entry → susceptible host. Breaking any link stops spread.

### Important terms

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Endemic | Constant usual presence of a disease in an area | Malaria in some districts |
| Epidemic | Cases clearly more than expected in an area and time | Cholera after floods |
| Pandemic | Epidemic spread over several countries or continents | COVID-19, H1N1 in 2009 |
| Outbreak | A small, localised epidemic | Food poisoning after a wedding meal |
| Sporadic | Scattered cases with no link | Tetanus cases |
| Incubation period | Time from entry of the agent to the first symptoms | Cholera hours to 5 days |
| Isolation | Separating **sick (infected)** people so they do not spread disease | TB ward, COVID isolation |
| Quarantine | Restricting movement of **healthy contacts** for the longest incubation period | Contacts of Ebola |
| Contact tracing | Finding, testing and watching people who met a case | COVID-19, TB |
| Morbidity | Illness in a population (incidence, prevalence) | Cases of dengue per 1000 |
| Mortality | Death in a population | Deaths due to TB per 1,00,000 |
| Carrier | Infected person without symptoms who spreads the agent | Typhoid carrier |

**Incidence** = new cases in a period ÷ population at risk. **Prevalence** = all existing cases at a time ÷ total population.

### Modes of transmission

```text
DIRECT                                INDIRECT
- Direct contact (touch, sex)         - Vehicle-borne (water, food, blood)
- Droplet (cough, sneeze < 1-2 m)     - Vector-borne (mosquito, fly, flea)
- Contact with soil (tetanus)         - Airborne (droplet nuclei, dust)
- Inoculation into skin (bites)       - Fomites (towels, utensils, toys)
- Transplacental (mother to foetus)   - Unclean hands and fingers
```

## 4.3 Respiratory infections

These spread mainly by **droplets** and close contact. Common prevention: vaccination, cough and sneeze etiquette, masks, hand hygiene, ventilation, isolation of cases.

### Chickenpox (varicella)

- **Agent:** varicella-zoster virus (VZV).
- **Spread:** droplets and contact with fluid from blisters.
- **Incubation:** about 14–16 days (range 10–21).
- **Features:** mild fever, then itchy rash that appears in crops — macule → papule → vesicle ("dew drop") → crust. Rash is mostly on the trunk (centripetal). Different stages are seen together. Infectious from 1–2 days before rash until all lesions crust.
- **Complications:** secondary skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis; later reactivation as **herpes zoster (shingles)**.
- **Prevention:** varicella vaccine (not in UIP); isolate till crusting; avoid aspirin in children (Reye's syndrome). Acyclovir for high-risk cases.

### Measles (rubeola)

- **Agent:** measles virus (paramyxovirus family). Highly infectious.
- **Spread:** droplets and airborne.
- **Incubation:** about 10 days to fever, about 14 days to rash.
- **Features:** fever with the "3 Cs" — cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; **Koplik's spots** (white spots inside cheeks); then red maculopapular rash starting behind ears and face, spreading down.
- **Complications:** pneumonia, diarrhoea, malnutrition, ear infection, encephalitis; rare late SSPE.
- **Prevention:** MR vaccine at 9–12 and 16–24 months; vitamin A for cases; isolation.

### Rubella (German measles)

- **Agent:** rubella virus.
- **Incubation:** 2–3 weeks.
- **Features:** mild fever, pink rash, swollen glands behind ears and at the back of the neck.
- **Danger:** infection in early pregnancy causes **congenital rubella syndrome** — cataract, deafness, heart defects, mental retardation.
- **Prevention:** MR vaccine; girls should be immune before pregnancy.

### Mumps

- **Agent:** mumps virus (paramyxovirus).
- **Incubation:** about 2–3 weeks (usually around 18 days).
- **Features:** fever, painful swelling of the **parotid glands** (one or both sides).
- **Complications:** orchitis (in adult males), meningitis, pancreatitis, deafness.
- **Prevention:** MMR vaccine (not in UIP, which uses MR).

### Influenza (including avian flu and H1N1)

- **Agent:** influenza virus types A, B, C (orthomyxovirus). Type A changes often: small changes (**antigenic drift**) cause yearly epidemics; big changes (**antigenic shift**) cause pandemics.
- **Incubation:** 1–3 days.
- **Features:** sudden fever, chills, headache, body ache, sore throat, cough, tiredness.
- **Avian flu (H5N1):** bird flu passing from infected poultry to humans; severe pneumonia; human-to-human spread is limited.
- **H1N1 ("swine flu"):** caused the 2009 pandemic; now a seasonal strain.
- **Treatment and prevention:** rest, fluids, paracetamol; **oseltamivir** for high-risk or severe cases; yearly influenza vaccine for elderly, pregnant women, health workers and chronic patients; cough etiquette.

### Coronavirus infections: SARS, MERS and COVID-19

| Disease | Virus | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SARS | SARS-CoV | Outbreak in 2002–03, starting in China; severe pneumonia |
| MERS | MERS-CoV | First seen in 2012 in the Middle East; camels are a source |
| COVID-19 | SARS-CoV-2 | Pandemic declared by WHO in March 2020 |

**COVID-19:** spreads by droplets, aerosols and contaminated surfaces; incubation 2–14 days (often about 5). Features — fever, dry cough, sore throat, tiredness, loss of smell and taste, breathlessness; severe pneumonia in elderly and people with diabetes, heart disease or poor immunity. Diagnosis: RT-PCR, rapid antigen test. Prevention: vaccination, masks, distancing, hand hygiene, ventilation, isolation, quarantine of contacts, contact tracing.

### Diphtheria

- **Agent:** *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* (Gram-positive rod); its **exotoxin** causes most damage.
- **Incubation:** 2–6 days.
- **Features:** sore throat, fever, a **greyish-white membrane** on tonsils and throat that bleeds when removed; swollen neck ("bull neck"); breathing obstruction.
- **Complications:** myocarditis, nerve paralysis.
- **Treatment:** diphtheria **antitoxin** plus penicillin or erythromycin; contacts get antibiotics.
- **Prevention:** pentavalent vaccine and DPT boosters, Td.

### Whooping cough (pertussis)

- **Agent:** *Bordetella pertussis* (Gram-negative).
- **Incubation:** 7–14 days.
- **Stages:** catarrhal (cold, most infectious) → paroxysmal (bouts of coughing ending in a "whoop", vomiting) → convalescent. Lasts weeks.
- **Complications:** pneumonia, convulsions, hernia, malnutrition; dangerous in infants.
- **Treatment:** azithromycin or erythromycin. **Prevention:** pentavalent/DPT vaccine.

### Meningococcal meningitis

- **Agent:** *Neisseria meningitidis* (Gram-negative diplococcus).
- **Spread:** droplets from carriers; crowding (hostels, camps, pilgrimages).
- **Incubation:** usually 3–4 days.
- **Features:** sudden fever, severe headache, vomiting, **neck stiffness**, light sensitivity, petechial rash, confusion; can kill within hours.
- **Treatment:** emergency hospital care with antibiotics (ceftriaxone, penicillin). **Close contacts** get chemoprophylaxis (rifampicin or ciprofloxacin). Meningococcal vaccines for travellers and outbreaks.

### Acute respiratory infections (ARI)

Infections of the nose, throat, ears, airways and lungs; **pneumonia** is a leading cause of death in children under 5.

- **Agents:** viruses (most colds); bacteria — *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae* type b.
- **Danger sign — fast breathing (child at rest):** 60 or more per minute below 2 months; 50 or more at 2–12 months; 40 or more at 1–5 years. Chest in-drawing, inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy → refer urgently.
- **Management:** colds — home care, fluids, no antibiotics; pneumonia — amoxicillin as per guidelines; severe — hospital.
- **Prevention:** breastfeeding, good nutrition, Hib and PCV vaccines, less indoor smoke, no smoking near children.

### Tuberculosis (TB)

- **Agent:** *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (acid-fast bacillus).
- **Spread:** droplet nuclei when a patient with lung TB coughs; infection is common, disease develops in a smaller number, more in people with HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, smoking.
- **Features of pulmonary TB:** **cough for 2 weeks or more**, fever (evening rise), night sweats, loss of weight and appetite, blood in sputum, chest pain. Extra-pulmonary TB affects lymph nodes, spine, brain, abdomen.
- **Diagnosis:** sputum microscopy, rapid molecular tests (CBNAAT/Truenat), chest X-ray.
- **Treatment (drug-sensitive TB, NTEP):** 2 months of isoniazid (H), rifampicin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), ethambutol (E), then 4 months of HRE, as daily fixed-dose combinations. Drug-resistant TB needs longer special regimens.
- **Prevention:** BCG at birth (protects against severe childhood TB), early diagnosis and full treatment, cough etiquette, ventilation, preventive therapy for contacts, nutrition support.
- **Pharmacist's role:** refer anyone with cough over 2 weeks; ensure the full course; counsel on red-orange urine (rifampicin), hepatitis signs, vision problems (ethambutol), pyridoxine with isoniazid; notify TB patients to the programme.

### Ebola virus disease

- **Agent:** Ebola virus (filovirus). Reservoir thought to be fruit bats.
- **Spread:** direct contact with blood and body fluids of patients or dead bodies; health workers at high risk.
- **Incubation:** 2–21 days.
- **Features:** sudden fever, weakness, muscle pain, then vomiting, diarrhoea, rash and bleeding; high death rate.
- **Prevention:** strict infection control with PPE, isolation, safe burial, contact tracing; a vaccine exists for outbreak use. Monitoring of travellers from affected countries.

## 4.4 Intestinal infections

Mostly spread by the **faeco-oral route** (5 Fs: faeces, fingers, flies, fluids, food). Common prevention: safe water, sanitary toilets, hand-washing with soap, food hygiene, fly control, vaccination where available.

### Poliomyelitis

- **Agent:** poliovirus types 1, 2, 3 (enterovirus).
- **Incubation:** usually 7–14 days.
- **Features:** most infections are silent; a few cause **acute flaccid paralysis** (sudden floppy weakness, usually of legs, asymmetric, no sensory loss).
- **Prevention:** OPV and IPV in UIP; Pulse Polio campaigns; surveillance of every case of acute flaccid paralysis in children under 15. India was certified **polio-free in 2014**; vaccination continues because the virus still exists elsewhere.

### Viral hepatitis

| Type | Spread | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Faeco-oral | Children; usually mild; vaccine available |
| E | Faeco-oral, water-borne epidemics | Very dangerous in pregnancy |
| B | Blood, sexual, mother to baby, needles | Carrier state, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver cancer; vaccine in UIP (birth dose) |
| C | Mainly blood (transfusion, needles) | Often chronic; curable with oral antivirals |
| D | Blood; only with B | Worsens hepatitis B |

**Features:** fever, nausea, loss of appetite, pain in right upper abdomen, dark urine, **jaundice**.
**Prevention:** safe water and food (A, E); vaccination, screened blood, sterile needles, safe sex (B, C, D). The National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme provides free testing and treatment.

### Cholera

- **Agent:** *Vibrio cholerae* (O1, including the El Tor biotype, and O139).
- **Incubation:** a few hours to 5 days (usually 1–2 days).
- **Features:** sudden profuse painless watery diarrhoea (**"rice-water stools"**), vomiting, rapid severe dehydration, muscle cramps; can kill within hours.
- **Treatment:** **rehydration** is life-saving — ORS; IV Ringer lactate in severe cases; antibiotics (doxycycline) shorten illness.
- **Prevention:** safe chlorinated water, sanitation, food hygiene, oral cholera vaccine in outbreaks.

### Acute diarrhoeal diseases

Three or more loose stools in 24 hours. Causes: rotavirus (commonest in infants), *E. coli*, *Shigella* (dysentery with blood), *Campylobacter*, protozoa.

**Assessing dehydration:** restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch goes back slowly → some dehydration; lethargic, unable to drink, skin pinch very slow → severe dehydration.

**Management:**

1. **Low-osmolarity ORS** (osmolarity 245 mOsm/L) — continue during diarrhoea.
2. **Zinc** for 14 days (10 mg/day under 6 months, 20 mg/day above 6 months).
3. Continue feeding and breastfeeding.
4. Antibiotics only for bloody diarrhoea (dysentery) or cholera; avoid anti-motility drugs in children.
5. Refer if danger signs.

**Prevention:** exclusive breastfeeding, rotavirus vaccine, safe water, hand-washing, sanitation, measles vaccine, vitamin A.

### Typhoid (enteric fever)

- **Agent:** *Salmonella* Typhi (paratyphoid: *S.* Paratyphi A, B).
- **Spread:** food and water contaminated by patients or **carriers** (bacteria live in the gall bladder).
- **Incubation:** usually 10–14 days.
- **Features:** fever rising step by step ("step-ladder"), headache, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhoea, coated tongue, relatively slow pulse, rose spots, enlarged spleen.
- **Complications:** intestinal bleeding and **perforation** (third week).
- **Diagnosis:** blood culture (first week), Widal test (later, less reliable).
- **Treatment:** antibiotics as per sensitivity (e.g. azithromycin, ceftriaxone); full course.
- **Prevention:** safe water and food, sanitation, treat carriers, typhoid vaccines (Vi polysaccharide, typhoid conjugate vaccine, oral Ty21a).

### Amoebiasis

- **Agent:** *Entamoeba histolytica* (protozoan); spread by **cysts** in contaminated food and water.
- **Features:** amoebic dysentery — stools with blood and mucus, abdominal cramps; may cause **amoebic liver abscess** (fever, painful enlarged liver).
- **Treatment:** metronidazole or tinidazole, followed by a luminal agent (e.g. diloxanide furoate) to clear cysts.
- **Prevention:** safe water (boiling kills cysts; normal chlorine doses may not), food hygiene, hand-washing.

### Worm infestations

| Worm | How it enters | Main effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roundworm (*Ascaris*) | Swallowing eggs from soil-contaminated food | Malnutrition, intestinal blockage |
| Hookworm (*Ancylostoma*, *Necator*) | Larvae penetrate skin of bare feet | Blood loss → iron-deficiency anaemia |
| Pinworm/threadworm (*Enterobius*) | Swallowing eggs; self-reinfection | Itching around anus at night |
| Whipworm (*Trichuris*) | Swallowing eggs | Diarrhoea, rectal prolapse |
| Pork tapeworm (*Taenia solium*) | Undercooked pork; eggs | Cysticercosis of brain → fits |

**Treatment:** albendazole 400 mg single dose (200 mg for children 1–2 years). **National Deworming Day** gives albendazole to children and adolescents twice a year.
**Prevention:** toilets, wearing footwear, hand-washing, clean nails, washing vegetables, cooking meat well.

### Food poisoning

Illness caused by eating food contaminated with microbes or their toxins; typically many people who ate the same meal fall ill.

| Organism | Typical food | Onset after eating | Features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *Staphylococcus aureus* (toxin) | Milk products, sweets handled by infected hands | 1–6 hours | Vomiting, cramps |
| *Bacillus cereus* | Reheated fried rice | 1–6 hours (vomiting type) | Vomiting |
| *Salmonella* | Eggs, poultry, meat | 12–24 hours or more | Fever, diarrhoea |
| *Clostridium perfringens* | Meat dishes kept warm | 8–24 hours | Diarrhoea, cramps |
| *Clostridium botulinum* | Badly canned or preserved foods | 12–36 hours | Descending paralysis, double vision; antitoxin needed |

**Prevention:** cook well, eat hot or refrigerate quickly, avoid keeping cooked food at room temperature, hand hygiene of food handlers, discard swollen cans. **Treatment:** ORS and supportive care; botulism is an emergency.

## 4.5 Arthropod-borne infections

Spread by **vectors** (mostly mosquitoes). Common prevention: remove breeding sites, insecticide-treated nets, repellents, full-sleeve clothes, window screens, larvicides and larvivorous fish, indoor residual spraying.

| Mosquito | Habits | Diseases |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Aedes aegypti* | Day biter; breeds in clean water in coolers, tyres, pots | Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever |
| Female *Anopheles* | Night biter; clean water | Malaria |
| *Culex* | Night biter; dirty water, drains | Filariasis (W. bancrofti), Japanese encephalitis |

### Dengue

- **Agent:** dengue virus, 4 serotypes (DENV 1–4).
- **Incubation:** usually 4–7 days (range 3–10).
- **Features:** sudden high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, severe muscle and joint pains ("break-bone fever"), rash, low platelet count.
- **Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums, restlessness, falling platelets → **dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome**; a second infection with another serotype raises the risk.
- **Treatment:** fluids, rest, **paracetamol only**; **avoid aspirin, ibuprofen and other NSAIDs** (bleeding risk).
- **Diagnosis:** NS1 antigen (early), IgM antibody.

### Malaria

- **Agent:** *Plasmodium vivax* (commonest in India), *P. falciparum* (most dangerous), *P. malariae*, *P. ovale*.
- **Vector:** female *Anopheles* mosquito.
- **Incubation:** about 12 days for falciparum and about 14 days for vivax (varies).
- **Features:** fever with **chills and rigors**, then sweating; headache, vomiting; anaemia, enlarged spleen. Vivax can relapse from dormant liver stages (hypnozoites).
- **Complications (falciparum):** cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, kidney failure, death.
- **Diagnosis:** rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or blood smear.
- **Treatment (national guidelines):** vivax — chloroquine for 3 days plus **primaquine for 14 days** (radical cure, check for G6PD deficiency where possible; not in pregnancy or infants); falciparum — **artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT)** plus a single dose of primaquine; severe malaria — injectable artesunate in hospital.
- **Prevention:** long-lasting insecticidal nets, indoor spraying, larvivorous fish (*Gambusia*, guppy), repellents, chemoprophylaxis for travellers.

### Filariasis (lymphatic filariasis)

- **Agent:** *Wuchereria bancrofti* (most cases, spread by *Culex*) and *Brugia malayi* (spread by *Mansonia*).
- **Features:** fever, swollen lymph nodes; years later **lymphoedema** of legs (elephantiasis), hydrocele.
- **Diagnosis:** night blood smear (microfilariae appear in blood at night), antigen tests.
- **Control:** **mass drug administration** in endemic areas — DEC + albendazole, or triple drug IDA (ivermectin + DEC + albendazole); care of swollen limbs (washing, skin care); hydrocele surgery; mosquito control.

### Chikungunya

- **Agent:** chikungunya virus (alphavirus); spread by *Aedes*.
- **Incubation:** usually 3–7 days.
- **Features:** sudden fever and **severe joint pain** that may last weeks or months (the name means "that which bends up"); rash.
- **Treatment:** rest, fluids, paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs until dengue is ruled out. **Prevention:** as for dengue.

## 4.6 Surface infections

### Trachoma

- **Agent:** *Chlamydia trachomatis*.
- **Spread:** eye discharge via fingers, towels, flies; poor water and hygiene.
- **Features:** chronic conjunctivitis with follicles → scarring of the eyelid → in-turned lashes (trichiasis) → corneal damage → **blindness**.
- **Control — SAFE strategy:** **S**urgery for trichiasis, **A**ntibiotics (azithromycin, tetracycline eye ointment), **F**acial cleanliness, **E**nvironmental improvement (water, sanitation). WHO validated India as having eliminated trachoma as a public health problem in 2024; surveillance continues.

### Tetanus

- **Agent:** *Clostridium tetani* — spores live in soil, dust and animal dung; enter through wounds (including the umbilical cord of newborns).
- **Incubation:** usually 6–10 days (range 3–21).
- **Features:** toxin causes painful muscle spasms — **lockjaw (trismus)**, fixed grin (risus sardonicus), arched back (opisthotonus), spasms triggered by noise or touch.
- **Neonatal tetanus:** from unclean cord cutting; prevented by Td for mothers and clean delivery. India was validated as having eliminated maternal and neonatal tetanus in 2015.
- **Treatment:** hospital care, human tetanus immunoglobulin, wound cleaning, metronidazole, muscle relaxants.
- **Prevention:** vaccination (pentavalent, DPT, Td); clean wounds; Td booster after dirty wounds.

### Leprosy (Hansen's disease)

- **Agent:** *Mycobacterium leprae*.
- **Spread:** prolonged close contact; droplets from the nose of untreated patients. Most people are naturally resistant.
- **Incubation:** long — on average several years (commonly 3–5).
- **Features:** pale or reddish skin patches with **loss of sensation**; thickened, tender nerves; weakness of hands and feet; deformities from repeated painless injury.
- **Types:** paucibacillary (PB, up to 5 patches) and multibacillary (MB, more than 5 patches or nerve involvement or positive smear).
- **Treatment — multidrug therapy (MDT):** rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine; WHO recommends the three drugs for both types, for 6 months (PB) and 12 months (MB). Free under the National Leprosy Eradication Programme.
- **Prevention:** early detection and MDT, examining contacts, single-dose rifampicin for contacts, fighting stigma, care of hands, feet and eyes.

## 4.7 Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) and HIV/AIDS

### Common STDs

| Disease | Agent | Main features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Syphilis | *Treponema pallidum* | Painless genital ulcer (chancre) → rash → late heart and brain damage; congenital syphilis in babies |
| Gonorrhoea | *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* | Pus discharge from urethra, painful urination; infertility |
| Chlamydia | *Chlamydia trachomatis* | Often silent; pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility |
| Chancroid | *Haemophilus ducreyi* | Painful genital ulcer, tender lymph nodes |
| Genital herpes | Herpes simplex virus (mainly HSV-2) | Painful recurrent blisters |
| Trichomoniasis | *Trichomonas vaginalis* | Frothy vaginal discharge, itching |
| Genital warts | Human papilloma virus (HPV) | Warts; some HPV types cause cervical cancer |

**Management:** **syndromic management** — treating the syndrome (urethral discharge, genital ulcer, vaginal discharge) at the first visit with standard drug kits; treat partners; counsel on condoms; test for HIV and syphilis.

### HIV/AIDS

- **Agent:** human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1, HIV-2), a **retrovirus** that destroys **CD4 T-lymphocytes**.
- **Spread:** unprotected sex (main route), infected blood and needles (injecting drug users), mother to child (pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding). **Not** spread by touching, hugging, sharing food, mosquitoes.
- **Window period:** time after infection when antibody tests may still be negative.
- **Course:** acute flu-like illness → long symptom-free period (years) → falling CD4 count → **AIDS** with opportunistic infections (TB is the commonest in India, oral thrush, pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis), weight loss, chronic diarrhoea.
- **Diagnosis:** HIV antibody tests at an Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre (ICTC), confirmed by approved testing strategy.
- **Treatment:** lifelong **antiretroviral therapy (ART)** started soon after diagnosis ("test and treat"); first-line in India is a fixed-dose combination of tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir. ART cannot cure but keeps the virus suppressed so the person lives a near-normal life and does not transmit it sexually.
- **Prevention:** condoms, safe blood, sterile needles, prevention of parent-to-child transmission (ART for pregnant women), post-exposure prophylaxis after needle-stick injury, awareness. National AIDS Control Programme (NACO).

## 4.8 Role of pharmacists in educating the public

1. **Explain how each disease spreads** and how to block it — posters, leaflets, talks in local language.
2. **Promote vaccination** and remind about due doses.
3. **Teach hygiene:** hand-washing, safe water, food safety, toilet use, cough etiquette, masks.
4. **Vector control advice:** emptying coolers weekly, nets, repellents.
5. **Early referral:** cough over 2 weeks, fever with chills, jaundice, bloody stools, danger signs in children, genital ulcers.
6. **Rational drug use:** no antibiotics for colds; paracetamol, not NSAIDs, in dengue; complete TB, leprosy and malaria courses; ORS and zinc for diarrhoea.
7. **Confidential, non-judgemental counselling** for STDs and HIV; supply condoms.
8. **Support national programmes** and report cases and adverse reactions.

## Remember

- Isolation = sick people; quarantine = healthy contacts.
- Epidemiological triad: agent, host, environment.
- Measles: Koplik's spots, 3 Cs; rubella in pregnancy → congenital rubella syndrome.
- Diphtheria: grey membrane, bull neck, antitoxin; pertussis: whoop, azithromycin.
- TB: cough ≥ 2 weeks; 2HRZE + 4HRE; BCG at birth.
- Cholera = rice-water stools → ORS; diarrhoea = low-osmolarity ORS + zinc 14 days.
- Dengue: Aedes day-biter, paracetamol only, no NSAIDs; malaria: Anopheles, vivax = chloroquine + primaquine 14 days.
- Trachoma SAFE; tetanus lockjaw; leprosy = anaesthetic patch + MDT.
- HIV: retrovirus, CD4 cells; TLD-based lifelong ART; not spread by casual contact.

# Unit 5: Health Systems and National Health Programmes in India

India runs many **national health programmes** to control diseases that affect large numbers of people. Most of them now work under the **National Health Mission (NHM)**. For each programme, learn four things: **objective → main components (functioning) → outcome → role of the pharmacist.**

> Programmes are renamed and updated from time to time. Learn the purpose and components; check the current name with your teacher.

## 5.1 Introduction to health systems

A **health system** includes all organisations, people and actions whose main purpose is to promote, restore or maintain health.

**WHO building blocks of a health system**

```text
 1. Service delivery        4. Access to essential medicines and vaccines
 2. Health workforce        5. Financing
 3. Health information      6. Leadership and governance
```

The pharmacist works mainly in block 4 (medicines) but supports all others.

**Health system in India (summary)**

| Level | Structure |
| --- | --- |
| Central | Ministry of Health & Family Welfare; DGHS; ICMR (research); NACO, Central TB Division and other programme divisions; CDSCO (drug regulation) |
| State | State health department; Directorate of Health Services; state drug controller |
| District | Chief Medical Officer; district hospital; district programme officers (TB, malaria, immunisation) |
| Block and village | CHC, PHC, sub-centre / Ayushman Arogya Mandir (Health and Wellness Centre); ANM, ASHA, Anganwadi worker |

**Ayushman Bharat** (2018) has two arms:

1. **Ayushman Arogya Mandirs** (earlier Health and Wellness Centres) — upgraded sub-centres and PHCs that give comprehensive primary care: maternal and child health, communicable diseases, screening for diabetes, high BP and common cancers, mental health, elderly care, free medicines and tests, yoga and wellness.
2. **Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY)** — health insurance cover for secondary and tertiary hospital care for poor and vulnerable families, usable in empanelled public and private hospitals.

**Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Janaushadhi Pariyojana (PMBJP)** — **Jan Aushadhi Kendras** sell good-quality **generic medicines** at low prices; run by a pharmacist. Also sells low-cost sanitary napkins.

## 5.2 National Health Mission and RMNCH+A

(See Unit 1 for NHM structure.) Under NHM, **RMNCH+A** (Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent health) uses a "continuum of care" approach.

| Life stage | Main schemes |
| --- | --- |
| Reproductive | Family planning — spacing methods, sterilisation, home delivery of contraceptives by ASHA |
| Maternal | Janani Suraksha Yojana (cash for institutional delivery), Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (free delivery, drugs, diet, transport), Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (free ANC check-up on a fixed day each month) |
| Newborn | Newborn care corners, sick newborn care units, home-based newborn care by ASHA |
| Child | Universal Immunization Programme, Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (screening for defects, deficiencies, diseases, developmental delays), diarrhoea and pneumonia control |
| Adolescent | Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram — nutrition, sexual and reproductive health, mental health, substance misuse; weekly iron–folic acid; menstrual hygiene |

**Pharmacist's role:** supply and counsel on IFA, ORS–zinc, contraceptives; check vaccination; refer high-risk pregnancies.

## 5.3 Universal Immunization Programme (UIP) and Mission Indradhanush

- **Objective:** protect children and pregnant women from vaccine-preventable diseases.
- **Components:** free vaccines on a national schedule (BCG, OPV, IPV, hepatitis B, pentavalent, rotavirus, PCV, MR, JE in endemic districts, DPT boosters, Td); cold chain; electronic vaccine stock monitoring (eVIN); AEFI surveillance; immunisation sessions at sub-centres and outreach.
- **Mission Indradhanush** (and its intensified rounds) — catch-up drives for children and pregnant women who missed doses.
- **Pulse Polio** campaigns and AFP surveillance maintain polio-free status.
- **Outcome:** polio eliminated; maternal and neonatal tetanus eliminated; rising full-immunisation coverage.
- **Pharmacist:** cold-chain care, reminders, counselling on side effects, dispelling myths, reporting AEFI.

## 5.4 National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP)

Earlier called the Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP); renamed NTEP in 2020.

- **Objective:** end TB in India, in line with the SDG target — fewer cases, fewer deaths, no catastrophic costs for families.
- **Strategy (Detect – Treat – Prevent – Build):**
  1. **Detect:** active case finding; rapid molecular tests (CBNAAT, Truenat); private-sector notification.
  2. **Treat:** free daily fixed-dose drugs; drug-resistant TB regimens; treatment supporters; adherence technology.
  3. **Prevent:** TB preventive therapy for contacts and people with HIV; BCG; airborne infection control.
  4. **Build:** **Ni-kshay** online case-based system; **Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana** (nutrition support through direct benefit transfer); **Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan** (community "Ni-kshay Mitras" adopt patients).
- **Pharmacist's role:** refer presumptive TB (cough ≥ 2 weeks); act as treatment supporter; ensure no gaps in treatment; counsel on side effects; notify TB cases; follow rules on sale of anti-TB drugs (record keeping).

## 5.5 National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP)

- **Objective:** reduce leprosy burden, prevent disability, and finally interrupt transmission.
- **Components:** early case detection (house-to-house campaigns, the Sparsh awareness campaign), free multidrug therapy (MDT) blister packs, single-dose rifampicin as post-exposure prophylaxis for contacts, disability prevention and medical rehabilitation (self-care, footwear, reconstructive surgery), fighting stigma.
- **Outcome:** leprosy eliminated as a public health problem at national level (prevalence below 1 per 10,000) in 2005; new cases still occur, so efforts continue.
- **Pharmacist:** recognise anaesthetic patches and refer; counsel on MDT (clofazimine causes skin darkening, rifampicin red urine); ensure adherence.

## 5.6 National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme (NVBDCP)

Covers **six** diseases: **malaria, dengue, chikungunya, lymphatic filariasis, Japanese encephalitis and kala-azar**. Now run by the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control.

- **Objective:** prevent and control vector-borne diseases; eliminate malaria, filariasis and kala-azar.
- **Components:**
  - Early diagnosis (RDT, microscopy) and complete treatment (ACT, chloroquine + primaquine).
  - Integrated vector management: long-lasting insecticidal nets, indoor residual spraying, larvivorous fish, source reduction, larvicides, fogging in outbreaks.
  - Mass drug administration for filariasis; morbidity management of swollen limbs and hydrocele.
  - JE vaccination in endemic districts; kala-azar case search and treatment.
  - Behaviour change communication; surveillance.
- **Pharmacist:** treat fevers only with proper diagnosis; paracetamol in dengue, avoid NSAIDs; counsel on complete antimalarial course; promote nets and repellents; tell people to empty water containers weekly ("dry day").

## 5.7 National AIDS Control Programme (NACP)

Run by **NACO** with State AIDS Control Societies.

- **Objective:** prevent new HIV infections and provide care, support and treatment to people living with HIV, reducing stigma.
- **Components:**
  - Targeted interventions for high-risk groups (sex workers, injecting drug users, men who have sex with men, truckers, migrants); condom promotion; needle–syringe exchange and opioid substitution therapy.
  - **ICTC** — free voluntary counselling and testing.
  - **PPTCT** — prevention of parent-to-child transmission.
  - **ART centres** — free lifelong antiretroviral therapy; link ART centres.
  - Blood safety (screened blood); STI clinics ("Suraksha clinics") with syndromic management.
  - IEC and the **HIV/AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017**, which protects people from discrimination.
- **Pharmacist:** supply condoms and needles discreetly, refer for testing, counsel on ART adherence and side effects, keep confidentiality, post-exposure prophylaxis awareness.

## 5.8 National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD)

Earlier called NPCDCS (cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and stroke).

- **Objective:** prevent and control common NCDs through health promotion, early diagnosis, management and referral.
- **Components:** population-based screening of adults (30 years and above) for **high BP, diabetes and common cancers (oral, breast, cervical)** at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs; NCD clinics at CHCs and district hospitals; free drugs; lifestyle counselling (diet, exercise, tobacco and alcohol); cardiac and cancer care units.
- **Pharmacist:** BP and sugar checks, counselling on adherence to antihypertensives and antidiabetics, lifestyle advice, insulin storage and injection technique.

## 5.9 National Mental Health Programme (NMHP)

- **Objective:** ensure minimum mental health care for all, especially the most vulnerable; integrate mental health with general health care; promote community participation.
- **Components:** **District Mental Health Programme (DMHP)** — outpatient and community services in districts; training of general doctors and health workers; suicide prevention; school and college mental health; **Tele-MANAS** (national tele-mental health helpline 14416); Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.
- **Pharmacist:** recognise depression and suicide risk, counsel on adherence to psychiatric drugs (they take weeks to act; do not stop suddenly), refer, store sedatives securely.

## 5.10 National Tobacco Control Programme (NTCP)

- **Objective:** create awareness about the harms of tobacco, help people quit, and implement tobacco control laws.
- **Components:** enforcement of **COTPA 2003** (no smoking in public places, no sale to minors or near schools, pictorial warnings, no advertising); tobacco cessation centres; national quitline; school programmes; ban on e-cigarettes (2019).
- **Pharmacist:** brief cessation advice (5 As), nicotine replacement therapy, refusing to stock or promote tobacco.

## 5.11 Other important national programmes

| Programme | Objective | Key components |
| --- | --- | --- |
| National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (NIDDCP) | Reduce goitre, cretinism and other IDD | Universal iodised salt; testing salt with kits; surveys; health education |
| Anemia Mukt Bharat | Reduce anaemia in children, adolescents, women of reproductive age and pregnant women | Age-wise IFA supplementation, deworming, testing and treating anaemia, fortified foods, behaviour change ("6 × 6 × 6" strategy) |
| National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI) | Reduce avoidable blindness | Free cataract surgery, school eye screening and free spectacles, eye banks, treatment of glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy |
| National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE) | Accessible, affordable care for elderly people | Geriatric clinics, home-based care, physiotherapy, regional geriatric centres |
| National Programme for Prevention and Control of Deafness (NPPCD) | Prevent avoidable hearing loss | Early detection, hearing aids, ENT services, training |
| National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP) | Combat hepatitis; eliminate hepatitis C | Free testing and treatment of hepatitis B and C; hepatitis B birth dose; safe injections and blood |
| Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) | Detect and respond early to outbreaks | Weekly reporting of epidemic-prone diseases (S, P, L forms), rapid response teams, labs; now on the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) |
| National Oral Health Programme | Improve oral health | Dental units at district level, awareness, oral cancer screening |
| National Deworming Day | Reduce worm load in children | Albendazole for children and adolescents in schools and Anganwadis, twice a year |
| POSHAN Abhiyaan / ICDS | Improve nutrition of children, pregnant and lactating women | Anganwadi supplementary nutrition, growth monitoring, take-home rations |
| National Programme on Climate Change and Human Health | Protect health from climate-related effects | Heat-wave action plans, preparedness |

## 5.12 Outcome of programmes — what India has achieved

- Smallpox eradicated (1977), guinea worm eradicated, **polio-free** certification (2014), maternal and neonatal tetanus eliminated (2015), yaws declared eliminated, trachoma eliminated as a public health problem (2024).
- Big falls in infant and maternal mortality since the 1990s.
- Much wider access to free ART, TB drugs and vaccines.

**Continuing challenges:** TB, anaemia and malnutrition, rising NCDs, mental health, antimicrobial resistance, urban slums, shortages of trained staff, out-of-pocket costs.

## 5.13 Role of pharmacists in national health programmes (general answer)

1. **Drug supply and logistics:** forecasting, storage (cold chain), stock records, avoiding stock-outs and expiry.
2. **Dispensing and counselling:** right dose, duration, side effects, adherence — especially TB, leprosy, HIV, malaria.
3. **Health education and IEC:** posters, health days (World TB Day, World AIDS Day, ORS Day), school talks.
4. **Screening and referral:** BP, sugar, BMI; cough, fever, anaemia signs, anaesthetic patches.
5. **Surveillance and reporting:** notify TB cases, report adverse drug reactions (Pharmacovigilance Programme of India) and AEFI.
6. **Rational use of medicines:** prevent antibiotic misuse; promote generics and Jan Aushadhi.
7. **Community link:** work with ASHAs, ANMs, Anganwadi workers and NGOs; join camps and campaigns.
8. **Emergencies and disasters:** emergency medicine supply, mass drug administration.

## Remember

- NHM = NRHM + NUHM; RMNCH+A = continuum of care.
- Ayushman Bharat = Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (primary care) + PM-JAY (hospital insurance).
- NTEP (renamed 2020): Detect–Treat–Prevent–Build; Ni-kshay portal; Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana.
- NVBDCP covers 6 diseases: malaria, dengue, chikungunya, filariasis, JE, kala-azar.
- NACP run by NACO: ICTC, PPTCT, ART centres; HIV/AIDS Act 2017.
- NP-NCD screens adults 30+ for BP, diabetes, oral/breast/cervical cancer.
- NMHP → DMHP, Tele-MANAS 14416; NTCP → COTPA 2003.
- Jan Aushadhi Kendras = generic medicines run by pharmacists.

# Unit 6: Pharmacoeconomics

Health resources (money, staff, medicines, beds) are always limited. **Pharmacoeconomics** helps decide which medicine or service gives the **best value** — the most health for the money spent. It is a short chapter (about 2 hours) but gives easy marks for definitions and the four types of analysis.

## 6.1 Introduction and definition

**Pharmacoeconomics** is the branch of health economics that identifies, measures and compares the **costs** and the **consequences (outcomes)** of drug therapy and pharmaceutical services, to help choose the most efficient option.

In simple words: *"Is drug A worth its price compared with drug B?"*

```text
        COSTS (inputs)                 CONSEQUENCES (outputs)
  drug price, doctor visits,   --->    cures, lives saved, fewer
  tests, hospital stay, lost           complications, better quality
  work days                            of life
              \                         /
               ---- compare the two ----
                 (cost per unit of outcome)
```

**Why it is needed:**

- Health spending keeps rising (new costly drugs, ageing population, chronic diseases).
- In India much health spending is **out of pocket**, so medicine prices push families into poverty.
- Governments, hospitals and insurers must choose what to buy and what to cover.

## 6.2 Basic terminologies

### Costs

| Type of cost | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Direct medical costs** | Money spent on medical goods and services | Medicines, doctor fees, tests, hospital stay, nursing, surgery |
| **Direct non-medical costs** | Money spent because of illness but not on medical care | Travel to hospital, food and stay for attendants, special diet, child care |
| **Indirect costs** | Loss of productivity because of illness or death | Lost wages, days off work or school, early death |
| **Intangible costs** | Non-money costs of pain and suffering | Pain, anxiety, grief, stigma; hard to measure |

Other cost terms:

- **Fixed cost:** does not change with the number of patients (building rent, equipment).
- **Variable cost:** changes with the number of patients (medicines, syringes).
- **Opportunity cost:** the value of the best alternative given up when resources are used for one purpose. Money spent on one costly drug cannot be used for vaccines.
- **Incremental cost:** extra cost of one option over another.
- **Average cost:** total cost ÷ number of units (patients).

### Outcomes (consequences) — the ECHO model

| Type | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **E**conomic | Outcomes counted in money | Costs saved, hospital days avoided |
| **C**linical | Medical events | Blood pressure controlled, infections cured, deaths avoided |
| **H**umanistic | The patient's view of health | Quality of life, patient satisfaction, functional status |

### Other key terms

- **Perspective:** whose costs are counted — the **patient**, the **provider** (hospital), the **payer** (government, insurer) or **society** (all costs; the broadest).
- **Utility:** a value for a health state from 0 (death) to 1 (perfect health), showing how people prefer that state.
- **QALY (quality-adjusted life year):** years of life × quality (utility).
  *Example:* 4 years lived at a utility of 0.5 = 2 QALYs.
- **DALY (disability-adjusted life year):** years of healthy life **lost** because of early death or disability (used to measure disease burden).
- **Efficacy vs effectiveness:** efficacy = how well a drug works in ideal trial conditions; effectiveness = how well it works in everyday practice.
- **Efficiency:** getting the most outcome for the resources used.
- **Discounting:** future costs and benefits are given a lower present value.
- **Sensitivity analysis:** repeating the calculation with different values (e.g. a higher drug price) to see whether the conclusion still holds.
- **Decision analysis (decision tree):** a diagram that maps choices, their chances and results, to compare options.

## 6.3 Types of pharmacoeconomic analysis

| Method | Outcome measured as | When used | Result expressed as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cost-minimisation analysis (CMA)** | Outcomes proven **equal** | Two drugs equally effective (e.g. brand vs generic) | Cheaper option is chosen |
| **Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA)** | Natural clinical units (mmHg lowered, cases cured, life-years gained) | Same kind of outcome, different effectiveness | Cost per unit of outcome; ICER |
| **Cost-benefit analysis (CBA)** | Money (outcomes converted into rupees) | Comparing programmes with different outcomes | Benefit-to-cost ratio; net benefit |
| **Cost-utility analysis (CUA)** | QALYs | When quality of life matters (chronic disease, cancer) | Cost per QALY gained |

### 1. Cost-minimisation analysis (CMA)

Used only when the outcomes of the options are shown to be the **same**. Then simply choose the lower cost.

*Example:* a branded and a generic amlodipine 5 mg tablet are bioequivalent. Brand costs ₹60 per strip and generic ₹15 — the generic is chosen.

### 2. Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA)

Compares costs with outcomes in **clinical units**.

*Example:*

| Antihypertensive | Cost per month (₹) | Patients reaching target BP |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drug A | 200 | 60 out of 100 |
| Drug B | 500 | 75 out of 100 |

- Cost per patient controlled: A = 200 × 100 ÷ 60 = about ₹333; B = 500 × 100 ÷ 75 = about ₹667.
- **Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER)** = (cost B − cost A) ÷ (effect B − effect A)
  = (₹50,000 − ₹20,000) ÷ (75 − 60) = ₹30,000 ÷ 15 = **₹2,000 per extra patient controlled** (for 100 patients a month).

Whether B is "worth it" depends on how much the payer is willing to pay for each extra controlled patient.

### 3. Cost-benefit analysis (CBA)

Both costs and outcomes are valued in **money**.

- **Benefit-to-cost ratio** = total benefits ÷ total costs (> 1 means worthwhile).
- **Net benefit** = benefits − costs (> 0 means worthwhile).

*Example:* a vaccination drive costs ₹10 lakh and prevents hospital and work-loss costs worth ₹40 lakh. Ratio = 4 : 1; net benefit = ₹30 lakh → worthwhile.

Drawback: putting a money value on life and health is difficult and controversial.

### 4. Cost-utility analysis (CUA)

A special kind of CEA where outcome is in **QALYs**.

*Example:* treatment X costs ₹1,00,000 and gives 2 extra QALYs → ₹50,000 per QALY. Treatment Y costs ₹60,000 and gives 1 QALY → ₹60,000 per QALY. X gives better value per QALY.

**Cost-of-illness study:** measures the total cost a disease puts on society (direct + indirect) — useful to show the burden of diseases such as diabetes or TB, though it does not compare treatments.

### Steps in a pharmacoeconomic evaluation

1. Define the problem and objective.
2. Choose the perspective.
3. Identify the options (alternatives) to compare.
4. Choose the type of analysis (CMA, CEA, CBA, CUA).
5. Identify and measure costs and outcomes.
6. Adjust for time (discounting) where needed.
7. Do the analysis (ratios, ICER, decision tree).
8. Do sensitivity analysis.
9. Present the results and make the decision.

## 6.4 Importance of pharmacoeconomics

1. **Formulary decisions:** hospitals choose which drugs to stock (drugs and therapeutics committees).
2. **Essential medicines lists:** the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) favours cost-effective drugs.
3. **Drug pricing:** price control of essential medicines by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) under the Drugs (Prices Control) Order.
4. **Insurance and government schemes:** deciding which treatments PM-JAY and state schemes should cover; **Health Technology Assessment in India (HTAIn)** studies cost-effectiveness for the government.
5. **Rational prescribing:** guiding doctors to equally effective, cheaper drugs; generic prescribing.
6. **Clinical guidelines:** standard treatment guidelines that consider cost.
7. **Drug development:** companies show value to get their drug used.
8. **Patients:** lower out-of-pocket spending; better adherence when medicines are affordable.

### Role of the pharmacist

- Suggest **generic substitutes** and Jan Aushadhi medicines where allowed.
- Avoid unnecessary and irrational drugs (e.g. antibiotics for colds, irrational fixed-dose combinations).
- Improve adherence — a medicine that is bought but not taken wastes money.
- Manage inventory to reduce expiry and wastage.
- Collect data on costs and outcomes for hospital studies.
- Counsel patients on the cheapest effective option.

### Limitations of pharmacoeconomic studies

- Costs and prices differ between countries, states and hospitals, so a foreign study may not apply in India.
- Intangible costs and quality of life are hard to measure; utilities depend on whose opinion is taken.
- Putting a money value on life (CBA) raises ethical objections.
- Trials measure efficacy in ideal patients; real-world effectiveness may be lower.
- Studies sponsored by manufacturers may be biased; results must be read critically.

### Quick worked QALY and DALY example

A patient with heart failure is expected to live 6 more years at a utility of 0.5 without a new drug (6 × 0.5 = 3 QALYs). With the drug he lives 8 years at 0.6 (8 × 0.6 = 4.8 QALYs). **QALYs gained = 1.8.** If the extra cost of the drug over those years is ₹90,000, the cost per QALY gained = 90,000 ÷ 1.8 = **₹50,000 per QALY**.

**DALY** = years of life lost (YLL) due to early death + years lived with disability (YLD). For example, if a disease causes 10 years of early death and 5 years of life with a disability weighted at 0.4, DALYs = 10 + (5 × 0.4) = 12. One DALY = one lost year of healthy life.

## Remember

- Pharmacoeconomics = costs vs consequences of drug therapy.
- Costs: direct medical, direct non-medical, indirect (lost productivity), intangible (pain).
- ECHO = Economic, Clinical, Humanistic outcomes.
- CMA → equal outcomes; CEA → clinical units, ICER; CBA → money, benefit-cost ratio; CUA → QALY.
- QALY = years × quality (0 to 1); DALY = healthy years lost.
- Uses: formulary, NLEM, NPPA pricing, insurance, HTAIn, generics.
